author: Γιάννης Βολιάτης
title: Macklemore και Kanye West: Δυο πολύ διαφορετικές περιπτώσεις
content:
Macklemore και Kanye West: Δυο πολύ διαφορετικές περιπτώσεις


Ό,τι χρειάζεται να ξέρουμε για το πως λειτουργεί το σιωνιστικό λόμπι στις ΗΠΑ, αλλά και η μεγαλύτερη απόδειξη ότι ο Σιωνισμός δεν έχει καμία σχέση με την “προστασία των Εβραίων” που ευαγγελίζεται, μπορεί να αναζητηθεί στην παρακάτω σύγκριση:


Όταν ο αφροαμερικανός (!) ράπερ Kanye West (ή “ye“ ή με όποιο άλλο γελοίο όνομα κυκλοφορεί αυτές τις μέρες) δήλωσε θαυμαστής του Αδόλφου Χίτλερ και ξεκίνησε να πουλάει merch με την Σβάστικα στο site του, καθώς και να φοράει αυτό το merch δημόσια -ενώ την ίδια ώρα ακριβώς έλεγε πως αγαπάει τους Εβραίους, έχει φίλους Εβραίους και κάτι τέτοια παλαβά που λένε και οι ομοφοβικοί για τους ομοφυλόφιλους για να καλύψουν την ομοφοβία τους- κανένας σιωνιστής επιχειρηματίας δεν κουνήθηκε από την θέση του, καμία συναυλία του δεν ακυρώθηκε, κανένα στάδιο των ΗΠΑ ιδιοκτησίας (φιλο)σιωνιστών επιχειρηματιών δεν τον banαρε. Μάλιστα, πολλοί έσπευσαν να πουν πως “έλα μωρέ, ο άνθρωπος απλά δεν είναι καλά, είναι ασταθής” κλπ. Κάτι χλιαρές δηλώσεις από κάποια κέντρα ανθρωπίνων δικαιωμάτων και αντιρατσιστικές ομάδες, που φυσικά και δεν είχαν καμία επίπτωση στην καριέρα του Kanye ή είχαν πολύ λίγη. Θα ήταν αστείο να συγκρίνει καν κάποιος τις αντιδράσεις των σιωνιστών στην υπόθεση αυτή, με την άψογα ενορχηστρωμένη επιχείρηση δυσφήμισης του Macklemore. Τελικά, τον Kanye (μάλλον) τον ανάγκασαν να βγει και να πει κάτι αστειότητες, του τύπου πως “είχε ένα τροχαίο ατύχημα που του επηρέασε τον μετωπιαίο λοβό” και τόσο καιρό που τα έλεγε όλα αυτά “δεν ήταν ο εαυτός του” (“Είμαι ένας άλλος ζω σε παράνοια, τον εαυτό μου βρίσκω σπάνια” που έλεγε και ο Νίνο).


Από την άλλη, ο Macklemore χρησιμοποίησε την προβολή του ως support artist μπροστά σε 70 χιλιάδες φαν του main event holder Ed Sheeran, ενός από τους πιο διάσημους -για κάποιον άγνωστο λόγο, όσο με αφορά- καλλιτέχνες στον κόσμο, για να μιλήσει υπέρ της Παλαιστίνης και ενάντια στην γενοκτονία που διαπράττει ο Σιωνισμός, ενώ την ίδια ώρα έκανε όσο πιο ξεκάθαρο γινόταν στο κοινό πως η κριτική στο Ισραήλ και τον Νετανιάχου δεν αποτελεί κριτική στους Εβραίους σαν λαό, θρησκεία, ό,τι είναι τέλος πάντων. Αμέσως βαπτίστηκε αντισημίτης και το επιχειρηματικό λόμπι που στηρίζει το Ισραήλ και στηρίζεται από αυτό, κίνησε γη και ουρανό για να αποκλειστεί από την συνέχεια του τουρ. Και τα κατάφερε επειδή ο Sheeran είναι πολιτικά ένα μαλάκιο χωρίς σπονδυλική στήλη.


Γιατί έγινε αυτό;


Πρώτον, γιατί ο Macklemore θα μπορούσε, σε 10 συναυλίες στο τουρ του Ed Sheeran, να απευθύνει αυτό το μήνυμα σε ένα εκατομμύριο περίπου ανθρώπους από κοντά, με ένα συνεκτικό λόγο και σε μορφή show, καθώς και σε εκατοντάδες εκατομμύρια άλλους, μέσα από video ή σε live μετάδοση. Αντίθετα, ο Kanye West, αν και μπορεί να επηρεάσει επίσης εκατομμύρια fans, δεν βγήκε (και δεν θα έβγαινε) με σβάστικα σε χιλιάδες κόσμο να τραγουδάει το “Erika” ή το “Das Mädchen unter der Laterne” και να εκπέμπει κάποιο συνεκτικό πολιτικό μήνυμα, κάτι για το οποίο δεν είναι ικανός φυσικά… Τα έλεγε και τα έκανε στο ίντερνετ, μπερδεμένα και λίγο μασημένα. Φανερά χαωμένος, ίσως από ντρόγκια, άγνωστο. Δεν ξεπλένουμε εδώ κανέναν φυσικά: Τα έλεγε συνειδητά, φορώντας σβάστικες έτσι; Και υμνώντας τον Χίτλερ. Και τα πούλησε και στο e-shop του. Λεπτομέρειες θα πει κανείς. Όχι εγώ.


Δεύτερον, ο Macklemore δεν έκανε καμία ΑΝΤΙΣΗΜΙΤΙΚΗ δήλωση. Δεν πρόσβαλε τον Εβραϊσμό σαν θρησκεία ή κουλτούρα. Αντίθετα μίλησε ξεκάθαρα ενάντια στην γενοκτονία, τον Σιωνισμό, τον Νετανιάχου. Έκανε δηλαδή κριτική, όχι στους Εβραίους, αλλά στην Κυβέρνηση, τις πολιτικές (αν η γενοκτονία μπορεί να ονομαστεί πολιτική) και την επίσημη ιδεολογία ενός κράτους με ισχυρά πολιτικά και οικονομικά συμφέροντα και ερείσματα, του πιο σημαντικού συμμάχου των ΗΠΑ και του Κεφαλαίου τους, που στις μέρες μας φαίνεται να εξαρτάται άμεσα από την συνέχιση της αγαστής συνεργασίας με τους γενοκτόνους. Όταν βάλλεται ο Σιωνισμός, όταν η λέξη “γενοκτονία” γίνεται κτήμα όλο και περισσότερων ανθρώπων και καθίσταται αποδεκτή σαν η πραγματική και ακριβής έννοια για αυτό που συμβαίνει στην Παλαιστίνη, δεν είναι φυσικά οι Εβραίοι που βάλλονται -όπως άλλωστε μας δίδαξαν και οι χιλιάδες αντισιωνιστές Εβραίοι ακτιβιστές κάθε ηλικίας και εθνικότητας, ανάμεσά τους και επιζώντες του Ολοκαυτώματος, σε όλο τον κόσμο και στις ΗΠΑ, με την σαφή δήλωση “not in our name”. Αντίθετα, αυτό που βάλλεται εδώ είναι η ιδεολογία πάνω στην οποία βασίζεται το γενοκτονικό κράτος. Και άρα, το ίδιο το Κράτος αυτό, αφού δεν υπάρχει Ισραήλ χωρίς …

author: Unknown
title: Anatomia di un furto: noi e Navier-Stokes
content:
In data 8 settembre, sul blog dell’azienda di intelligenza artificiale OpenAI è comparso un post il quale sostiene che un modello di IA generativa non disponibile al pubblico – ed evidentemente più potente del loro ultimo modello: GPT-6 Astra – abbia risolto le equazioni di Navier-Stokes, uno dei sette problemi del millennio.


L’equazione di Navier-Stokes è l’equazione fondamentale della dinamica dei fluidi classica e descrive un fluido (come l’aria o l’acqua) in termini newtoniani, ossia applicando il secondo principio della dinamica (F=ma) a un fluido incomprimibile, visto, approssimando, come oggetto continuo e non come insieme di atomi. Si tratta di un sistema di equazioni differenziali le cui soluzioni sono oggetti continui in uno spazio a infinite dimensioni e servono per calcolare la variazione di velocità di un fluido a partire dal gradiente di pressione, dalla viscosità e dalle forze esterne (gravità o forze applicate). Sono concetti che nascono tra 700 e 800, ma nonostante l’apparente semplicità concettuale sono equazioni di cui non si riesce a scrivere una soluzione analitica per la versione generale, per cui è necessario utilizzare ulteriori approssimazioni per semplificare dei termini (approssimazioni che per la maggioranza dei casi sono più che sufficienti, specialmente in campo ingegneristico). Solo nel XX secolo è stato dimostrato che delle soluzioni generali esistono. La domanda irrisolta rimane: se io fisso le mie condizioni iniziali può accadere che la mia soluzione a un certo punto sviluppi una singolarità? Ossia è possibile che la soluzione mi dia una velocità infinita in un tempo finito (cioè ad energia finita)? 


Il problema del millennio riguarda dunque lo status di regolarità di questa equazione, cioè la validità di questo modello classico e delle approssimazioni sopra citate. Questo problema è risolvibile in due modi: 1. dimostrando positivamente che non si possono sviluppare delle singolarità; 2. trovando una situazione che con determinate condizioni produce questa singolarità. Degli agenti AI utilizzati metà sono stati messi a risolvere il problema nel primo modo, metà nel secondo. Sono stati proprio questi ultimi a riuscire.


Dopo queste minime coordinate per intendere al meglio lo spessore del problema, possiamo discutere di ciò che è successo.


La faccenda è tutto fuorché priva di zone d’ombra. In primis, soprattutto per gli appassionati, nonostante OpenAI abbia fornito le dimostrazioni a queste equazioni, bisognerà aspettare almeno due anni affinché il Clay Mathematics Institute approvi la dimostrazione.


In secundis, in contemporanea alla dichiarazione di OpenAI, lo scienziato Tristan Buckmaster ha

contestato

 l’azienda big tech sostenendo che l’azienda ha sostanzialmente rubato le idee a lui e ad un altro scienziato: Levent Alpöge.


Buckmaster sostiene che recentemente lui e Alpöge avevano reso pubblico tre risultati che riguardavano le equazioni di Navier-Stokes, basandosi su un programma di ricerca redatto da Diego Còrdoba e Luis Martìnez-Zoroa. Lo stesso programma da cui OpenAI sarebbe partito. Buckmaster e Alpöge non nascondono l’utilizzo estensivo di Large Language Model per farsi aiutare nella ricerca, tuttavia sostenendo che le dimostrazioni fornite dalle IA erano “orrende” e più vicine al genere del “AI slop”.


La controversia inizia il 3 settembre con Buckmaster che scrive ad un matematico di OpenAI poiché girava voce che dentro Anthropic – azienda programmatrice di Claude e competitor diretto di OpenAI – si fosse risolto uno dei problemi del millennio e che informazioni sul progresso dei due matematici fossero passate ad OpenAI. Senza entrare troppo nei dettagli tecnici, un problema di dimostrazione matematica può essere “attaccato” in modi differenti e vedere infine se porta ad un risultato e quanto è elegante. Il modo in cui Buckmaster e Alpöge hanno iniziato a lavorare al problema era un modo che stavano sperimentando solo loro due. Tuttavia, un altro scambio tra Alpöge e OpenAI ha messo in luce il fatto che la scoperta interna dell’azienda big tech ha seguito lo stesso “fronte d’attacco” fornendo al LLM soltanto un prompt che illustrava il problema. I due matematici vengono a sapere che è stato generato pochi giorni prima, ovvero quando è circolata l’informazione che ci fossero grandi progressi sulle equazioni di Navier-Stokes. OpenAI, in seguito, non è stata chiara con Buckmaster se e quanto il loro modello è stato addestrato con i lavori che i due matematici …

author: newsroom
title: Αστυνομικοί με πολιτικά επιχείρησαν να πάρουν δύο μικρότερα παιδιά της οικογένειας από την υπόθεση Κολωνού
content:
Σύνδεσμος δημοσίευσης:

Αστυνομικοί με πολιτικά επιχείρησαν να πάρουν δύο μικρότερα παιδιά της οικογένειας από την υπόθεση Κολωνού


Μια νέα καταγγελία για ακραία συμπεριφορά αστυνομικών του Α.Τ. Κολωνού, αυτή τη φορά εναντίον των μικρών αδερφιών της επιζώσας από τη γνωστή υπόθεση

τράφικινγκ με πρωταγωνιστή τον Ηλία Μίχο

, δημοσιοποιεί η

Επιτροπή Αλληλεγγύης στη 12χρονη

:


ΚΑΤΑΓΓΕΛΙΑ ΕΠΑΝΑΤΡΑΥΜΑΤΙΣΜΟΥ ΔΥΟ ΑΝΗΛΙΚΩΝ ΠΑΙΔΙΩΝ


ΤΗΣ ΟΙΚΟΓΕΝΕΙΑΣ ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΥΠΟΘΕΣΗ ΤΟΥ ΚΟΛΩΝΟΥ


Σήμερα 17/9 περίπου στις 13.00 το μεσημέρι, δύο άνδρες με πολιτικά που διατείνονταν ότι είναι αστυνομικοί και φέρουν εισαγγελική απόφαση επιχείρησαν να απαγάγουν τα δύο μικρότερα παιδιά (12 και 11 ετών) της οικογένειας από την υπόθεση του Κολωνού.


Συγκεκριμένα, οι δύο άντρες πλησίασαν τα ανήλικα παιδιά την ώρα που εκείνα επέστρεφαν με τη μητέρα τους από το σχολείο, προσπάθησαν να τα παρεμποδίσουν να μπουν στο σπίτι και επιχείρησαν να τα οδηγήσουν σε ΙΧ αυτοκίνητο. Στις επαναλαμβανόμενες εκκλήσεις της μητέρας αρνήθηκαν να επιδείξουν τόσο τις αστυνομικές τους ταυτότητες, όσο και την εισαγγελική απόφαση που όριζε τη μεταφορά των παιδιών. Σκοπός τους είπαν πως ήταν η μεταφορά των παιδιών στο Α.Τ. Κολωνού για τη διενέργεια εξετάσεων για σεξουαλικώς μεταδιδόμενα νοσήματα, ενώ τα απείλησαν με μεταφορά και στο χαμόγελο του παιδιού. Όπως ήταν επόμενο τα παιδιά φώναζαν και έκλαιγαν τρομαγμένα. Η οικογένεια και ο κόσμος από τις γύρω πολυκατοικίες ενεπλάκησαν για να τα προστατέψουν και να σταματήσουν την κακοποιητική μεταγωγή τους.


Μετά από τηλεφωνική επικοινωνία με τον διοικητή του ΑΤ Κολωνού αποδείχθηκε πως οι άνδρες ήταν όντως αστυνομικοί και υπήρχε πράγματι εισαγγελική παραγγελία, από την οποία μένει να απαντηθεί το ερώτημα αν ήταν αυτός ο κατάλληλος τρόπος εκτέλεσης της απόφασής της.


Δηλώνουμε σε κάθε τόνο.


Η βία στα παιδιά δε θα περάσει.


Αν το κράτος αγωνιά για το αν δύο μικρά παιδιά κακοποιούνται, η λύση δεν είναι να τα επανατραυματίζει ξανά και ξανά. Να τα προσεγγίζει απειλητικά με όρους απαγωγής και να τα απειλεί πως θα απομακρυνθούν από το οικογενειακό τους πλαίσιο σε περίπτωση μη συμμόρφωσης. Το κράτος για μια ακόμη φορά λειτουργεί κακοποιητικά απέναντι σε παιδιά ήδη πολλαπλώς τραυματισμένα. 


Το κράτος φαίνεται να αντιλαμβάνεται τα παιδιά ως ξερά σώματα, πιόνια για πολιτικά παιχνίδια. Θεωρεί ότι μπορεί χωρίς τα απαραίτητα έγγραφα και τις νόμιμες διαδικασίες να στέλνει αστυνομικούς με πολιτικά να παίρνουν παιδιά απ’ το σπίτι τους. Μπροστά στη δική που πλησιάζει, προσπαθούν να εκφοβίσουν την οικογένεια με κάθε τρόπο.                          


17/9/2026


Επιτροπή αλληλεγγύης στη 12χρονη 


Υπενθυμίζεται ότι παρόμοιες συμπεριφορές από αστυνομικούς έχουν ξανασυμβεί σε σχέση με αυτή την υπόθεση:


Καταγγελία: Το κράτος συνεχίζει τη δόλια τακτική του απέναντι στη 12χρονη


Αστυνομικοί με πολιτικά επιχείρησαν να πάρουν δύο μικρότερα παιδιά της οικογένειας από την υπόθεση Κολωνού

author: Redazione_web
title: Sciopero Generale 30 ottobre / manifestazioni 31 ottobre. L’internazionale anarcosindacalista promuove una mobilitazione contro le guerre
content:
La ICL-CIT, organizzazione internazionale a cui aderisce l’Unione Sindacale Italiana, ha lanciato un appello per due giornate di mobilitazione contro il militarismo e contro tutte le guerre.


L’USI-CIT accoglie l’appello dell’organizzazione internazionale di cui è parte, condividendone le preoccupazioni per l’attuale situazione globale e per le politiche del governo italiano che non si oppongono alle guerre in corso, quando non le legittimano o perfino le favoriscono.


L’USI proclama lo sciopero generale per il giorno 30 ottobre 2026 di tutto il personale dipendente pubblico e privato per l’intera giornata.


Scioperiamo contro il militarismo, contro l’aumento delle spese militari e della produzione di armamenti; contro l’economia di guerra e il conseguente peggioramento delle condizioni delle lavoratrici e dei lavoratori; contro l’esportazione di armi, sia vendute che cedute gratuitamente, in particolare in paesi coinvolti in conflitti; contro la militarizzazione della società.


Scioperiamo per l’azzeramento delle spese militari e l’investimento dei risparmi derivanti dall’abbattimento di tali spese in politiche sociali nell’ambito di sanità, scuola, edilizia pubblica e tutto ciò che costituisce lo stato sociale; per il ritiro di tutte le spedizioni militari all’estero; per la smilitarizzazione della società: basta militari nelle scuole e nelle strade!


Per i vigili del fuoco lo sciopero riguarderà solo il primo turno, mentre vengono esclusi dalla presente proclamazione i lavoratori e le lavoratrici dei seguenti settori: Trasporto pubblico locale, Trasporto aereo, Trasporto ferroviario, Trasporto marittimo. Si invitano organizzazioni sindacali conflittuali con presenza in tali settori dei trasporti ad analoga proclamazione dello sciopero generale nella stessa giornata.


L’organizzazione internazionale che ha promosso questa mobilitazione, la ICL-CIT, acronimo di Confederazione Internazionale del Lavoro (in lingua inglese e spagnola), si costituisce nel Congresso Internazionale delle organizzazioni anarcosindacaliste che si è tenuto a Parma nel 2018.


In questo momento aderiscono alla CIT le organizzazioni sindacali USI (USI CIT Italia), CNT (Spagna), IWW-NARA (Nord-America), IP (Polonia), FAU (Germania), CNT-F (Francia), IWW-WISERA (Gran Bretagna), ESE (Grecia), FORA (Argentina). Recentemente hanno chiesto l’adesione anche la FOB (Brasile) e la FGWM (Birmania). I principi basilari della CIT sono quelli dell’anarcosindacalismo definiti nello Statuto interno, in coerenza con i principi fondativi della Prima Internazionale per cui “l’Emancipazione sarà opera dei lavoratori stessi”. Attualmente ricopre l’incarico di Segretaria Anna Gussetti per la USI CIT, un incarico che dopo due anni di mandato, per il principio della rotazione, sta volgendo al termine, ed è previsto il passaggio della nuova Segreteria alla IP (Polonia).


Siamo di fronte ad una grave situazione internazionale, in cui l’industria delle armi e il loro commercio stanno imponendo le linee politiche utili ai loro profitti, promuovendo guerre in continua espansione sempre più pericolose, a rischio di una catastrofe umanitaria, provocando il progressivo impoverimento delle classi lavoratrici. In tale situazione le organizzazioni associate alla CIT hanno approvato la proposta di USI per una mobilitazione internazionale contro la guerra.


Dal 25 al 27 settembre si terrà in Italia, a Massenzatico, in provincia di Reggio Emilia, il Congresso straordinario della CIT. Chiediamo alla compagna Anna Gussetti, che a settembre termina il suo mandato di Segretaria CIT in rappresentanza dell’USI, che cosa ritiene di significativo sia stato realizzato in questa fase: “In questo periodo la Confederazione si è concentrata sul sostegno concreto (anche economico) alle lotte portate avanti a livello nazionale dai singoli sindacati della CIT (e non solo da essi) e in alcuni casi abbiamo dato vita a mobilitazioni partecipate in più paesi. L’evidente utilità di tali iniziative ha consentito inoltre di aumentare il numero dei sindacati aderenti all’internazionale”. Domandiamo allora quali siano le aspettative sul Congresso straordinario della CIT che si svolgerà a fine settembre: “Il Congresso straordinario è stato richiesto dall’USI soprattutto per risolvere alcuni problemi organizzativi interni. Il funzionamento della CIT è piuttosto macchinoso, come è logico sia in un’organizzazione federalista e libertaria, ma a volte i suoi meccanismi rischiano di frenare …

author: Kate Qiyu Chen
title: Teaching African Literature in a Small American Town
content:
1.


One week after returning to China for the summer, I came down with a cold and a fever.


During my recovery, I shut off every channel through which work could reach me, as though I were gradually drifting away from a particular identity and the time-space it inhabited. I watched Japanese anime and read Chinese books. For a while, my English and Kiswahili went to sleep. My e-reader, loaded with more than a dozen books for next semester’s research plans, had not been turned on for a week. It, too, lay quietly asleep.


On the first day after I recovered, with little to do—or perhaps nudged by preparations for next semester’s teaching—I returned to my summer reading:

Nnedi Okorafor

‘s novel

Lagoon

. Her leaping prose and fluid storytelling felt like seawater, like waves, and even more like the mist that, in the novel, hangs over Lagos. The book awakened my memories. It awakened another identity within me, along with the time-space in which it dwells.


2. 


“What is your research?”

“African literature.”


Just these two words—“Africa” and “literature”—are enough to trigger a cascade of questions.


One summer during my PhD, back in China, I attended a dinner party organized by my parents’ generation. A middle-aged uncle, cigarette in hand and one leg crossed over the other, looked at me and asked: “African literature? Does Africa even have literature? When you go to Africa, don’t you just see elephants and lions?”


Before I could respond, he had already launched into his grand theory about whether Chinese culture or Western culture was superior, as if he had forgotten what he had asked in the first place: African literature.


After I started working, I met an Asian professor of East Asian languages. When she first heard my research area, she gave me the same look of surprise: “African literature? Isn’t that something only Black scholars study? How did you end up working on this?”


From my PhD years to my current job, I have answered the question of why I study African literature countless times.


For many people, an Asian woman working on African literature still seems difficult to imagine. When Asian women do not choose fields, they are expected to enter—such as East Asian languages and literatures or Asian American studies—their academic position often becomes difficult to locate epistemologically. Many people seem uncertain how to make sense of my presence.


In my first month at work, I was constantly borrowing books from the library, returning them, buying coffee, and writing. Because I looked young, I was almost always mistaken for a student.


“What year are you in? What do you study?”

“Oh—you’re a professor?”

“Oh—you’re the new faculty member in Africana Studies?”

Faced with a series of questions and exclamation marks, I always find myself needing to explain. My skin color and my research form a kind of mismatch in the eyes of others, as if a sandbag were tied to my legs—heavy, weighing down every step I take.


Terms like Black, African, Africana,

Āfēilìjiā

, all seem closely tied to the idea of “Blackness.” On one level, this connection is entirely understandable. In North America, Black Studies emerged out of student movements in California in the late 1960s, when students demanded that university curricula pay greater attention to people of color in the United States. Black Studies not only opened up systematic academic inquiry into Black history and culture but also laid the groundwork for other ethnic and minority studies in higher education, such as Asian American Studies, Latinx Studies, Indigenous Studies, and Gender Studies. In the United Kingdom, Canada, and other Western countries, Black Studies developed along its own historical trajectories, while also intersecting with and resonating with the North American experience.


The formation of Black Studies was never simply about establishing a stable academic discipline within the university. It carried a revolutionary and radical charge, reflecting Black students’ deep concern with racial equality and ongoing struggles for social justice. At the time of its emergence as a field, the wounds and legacies of slavery still deeply structured social reality; African nations had gained political independence one after another, yet this had not necessarily translated into improved living conditions for their populations; and apartheid in South Africa remained firmly in place. Against this historical backdrop, Black Studies was envisioned …

author: ROAPE
title: Food security or seed capture? The colonial potato and Africa’s seed wars
content:
It all begins with a potato. Not the kind that nourishes a nation in textbook stories, but a colonial potato. This potato was shipped, tested, rationed, pushed through mission gardens and military supply lines, and ultimately sold as progress. Tracing that potato across Nigeria’s highlands leads to today’s disputes over seed, debt, law, and who decides what African farmers cultivate. 


Seeds are not just seeds. They carry memory, labour, taste, law, power, and often, debt.

The colonial potato scheme in Nigeria

 is significant because it shows how dependency on seeds can develop even before it is codified in law. Nowadays, discussions about seed sovereignty in Africa often centre on patents, plant breeders’ rights, certified seed laws, and agribusiness. However, colonial Nigeria reveals an older method of control: emergency.       


In the 1930s and 1940s, British officials transformed the

Jos and Mambila Plateaus

 into experimental sites for growing potatos. Initially, the scheme was small and awkward, driven by European miners, missionaries, and colonial officers seeking familiar food. Then, the Second World War (1939-1945) changed everything. Supply routes were disrupted, troops needed food, and Nigerian highland farmers were forcibly integrated into a larger imperial food plan. An agricultural experiment became part of the British empire’s war effort.


An anthropological base map of Plateau Province reproduced from C.G. Ames, The Gazetteers of Plateau Province, 1932 (Copy in Nigerian National Archives, Kaduna)


The highlands were ideal for the crop. Potatos thrive in cooler conditions, and Jos and Mambila provided the climate colonial agronomists desired. However, these areas were not empty spaces waiting for improvement. They were inhabited, farmed, and politically complex societies with their own crops, markets, and knowledge systems.


Colonial rule altered the dynamics in these regions. Tin mining on the Jos Plateau attracted workers, administrators, and settlers. Demand for European foods increased. Potatos, once a garden crop for expatriates and mission stations, began to seem valuable to the colonial state.


Starting in the 1930s, British

officials based in Nigeria began importing seed potatos from Ireland, Britain, Europe, South Africa, the Canary Islands, and the United States.

 Mission stations cultivated the potatos. District heads distributed the seed. Farmers cautiously tried the crop, incorporating it into local routines where it made sense while rejecting it when it didn’t. The potato became a means of power.


This did not mean that older crops and seed systems disappeared. There was no formal ban, and local farmers continued to grow, save, and exchange seed in various ways. The scheme worked in subtler ways: it altered the rewards. Access to land, labour, credit, official support, and markets began to favour the colonial crop. Imported seed was seen as improved, while farmer-saved seed and local knowledge were pushed to the sidelines. Over time, diverse and adaptable seed systems were narrowed, though not completely erased, by a supply chain prioritising mines, mission stations, military demands, and imperial markets.


Before the Second World War, the scheme was no great success. Some farmers thought potatos were poisonous. Others saw no reason to cultivate a crop with a limited, European-dominated market. A 1937 attempt to sell imported ‘Great Scott’ seed potatos to the Jos Native Authority ended poorly: half went unsold, the remainder was given away, and the scheme lost money.


War transformed failure into urgency. The empire needed food close to military outposts. It aimed to save cargo space and lessen reliance on disrupted shipping routes. Suddenly, potatos on the Mambila and Jos Plateau became crucial.


The war economy and the creation of dependency


Production surged from around

90 tons at the beginning of the war in 1939 to about 1,200 tons by 1943. Seed stores and experimental stations emerged throughout Kagoro, Zonkwa, Kurmin Biri, and Riyom

. Colonial science advanced rapidly, too: London-based Kew scientists devised ways to transport sprouting ‘eyes’ of potatos instead of whole tubers, facilitating a steady supply from outside.


Wartime officials did not establish an independent Nigerian seed system; they created a supply chain. Farmers were encouraged to boost production. Yet, this authority remained elsewhere: seed, disease control, imports, and markets remained …

author: Moataz Hagag
title: Farming permit gridlock at Lake Nasser reignites demands for Nubian right of return
content:
Five months ago, a group of young men from the Nubian village of Daboud tried to apply for permits at the Lake Nasser Development Authority to grow watermelons along the lake’s shore. 


They were told to return in August or early September, when applications are typically open.

But when they did, they were told there were no permits available, even though other farmers

were working in the area.


The group then went to the

 Egyptian Border Guard Corps,

 but were unable to meet the official they were seeking. During that time, they saw other people entering and leaving with permits for various activities, said one of the young men, who spoke to Mada Masr on condition of anonymity. “We sat there for three hours until the place cleared out and we were [the only ones] left,” he said.


Three days later, the young men took things into their own hands.

They published a video online on September 4, calling for a Nubian mass mobilization

conference

 the following week to discuss their demands and the Nubian community’s role in developing the Lake Nasser region.

 


Suddenly, officials, lawmakers and intermediaries began to reach out to them, offering two agricultural wells and fishing opportunities, while discussing arrangements for meetings with government officials and security agencies, the source, who also helped organize the conference, told Mada Masr. “Before the video, nobody was talking to us,” he said. 


With the offers came pressure. The organizers simultaneously began to receive threats to postpone or cancel the event, he added, declining to identify those behind the threats.

They were told they could meet officials from the

Future of Egypt

 for Sustainable Development Authority,

 an agency headed by Air Force Pilot Colonel Bahaa Ghanem and which oversees major agricultural and development projects, on the condition that they postpone the conference.


But the organizers refused. “We can negotiate and still not cancel or postpone the conference,” the organizer said. “We promised the Nubian people.”


Nubian women carrying their children and belongings after being displaced from one of their villages in Nubia during the repeated displacement campaigns that began in 1898 with the construction of the Aswan Low Dam. Source: Nubian Egyptian Union in France.


Daboud’s new mobilization over access to land and economic opportunities stems from the displacement of Nubian communities from their ancestral lands and the longstanding demands for return that followed successive waves of displacement beginning in 1898.


The new push — including the Popular Nubian Conference convened on September 10 — has brought the historical struggle back into the conversation in recent days, with the government moving in parallel to address outstanding reparations for Nubians displaced by the High Dam — an issue that Nubian leaders have insisted is separate from their constitutional right of return.


***


The Nubian right of return was explicitly recognized in the 2014 Constitution, with Article 236 stipulating that the state is responsible for developing the region and allowing Nubians back into their ancestral lands by 2024. 


That same year, the Transitional Justice Ministry formed a committee to prepare a draft law concerning Nubia’s development and the community’s resettlement, which included Nubian representatives alongside official entities.


Article 236 of the Constitution requires the government to facilitate the return of Nubian citizens to their ancestral homeland.


But the state has never followed through on that commitment.

Instead, it undermined the Nubian return project through two

presidential decrees

, issued in 2014 and 2016, that placed historically Nubian lands under state control.


The first, Presidential Decree 444/2014, designated parts of the border region as military zones where civilians could not live, effectively barring Nubians from returning to 16 of their historic villages. Two years later, Presidential Decree 355/2016 allocated 922 feddans of state-owned land to the New Toshka development project, including the site of the historic Nubian village of Furkund. 


Those decisions

triggered

 a wave of Nubian

organizing

. In November 2016, security forces prevented the 25-car Nubian Return Caravan from reaching Toshka, where participants planned to protest Furkund’s inclusion in the state-backed development project.

The

barricade

turned into a four-day sit-in on the Aswan-Abu Simbel …

author: Adebayo Afolabi
title: Nigeria’s Accountability Crisis Is Fueling Every Other Political Crisis
content:
On March 23, 2026, a Federal High Court in Abuja handed down a 72 year sentence, to be served as eight years concurrently, to Chukwunyere Nwabuoku, the former acting Accountant General of the Federation, for laundering funds while he ran finance for the Ministry of Defence. At first glance, it looks like a rare victory for accountability. It is also, on closer look, proof of how unusual accountability has become.

A review of 393 corruption cases

 involving Nigerian public officials between 2013 and 2026 found that only 144 ever reached a final judgment. Roughly six in ten sit unresolved, some for over a decade, while the accused keep their freedom, their assets, and often their offices.


 


National Assembly Complex, Abuja


Nigeria’s deepest political crisis is not corruption, poverty, or insecurity on their own. It is the near total absence of consequences for the people who cause them. Officials are investigated and never tried. Governors face removal proceedings, only for the process to be overtaken by court rulings or political bargains. Security failures repeat because senior officials rarely face consequences for them. Each of these failures compounds the next, and all of them trace back to one missing ingredient: a cost for getting caught.


Every scandal that dies quietly teaches the next official that the system will absorb the loss. That lesson shapes how public money is spent, how elections are contested, and how much faith citizens place in their own government, right as the country heads toward the 2027 elections.


A culture built over decades


Nigeria’s tolerance for unpunished power did not start with this republic. Decades of military rule normalized the idea that those in charge answer to no one, and the civilian government since 1999 inherited that habit. Weak courts, a politicized Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, legislative godfathers who make and unmake governors, and a public grown tired of outrage have all helped the pattern outlive the dictatorships that produced it.


The 1999 Constitution promises, under Section 14(2)(b), that the security and welfare of the people shall be the primary purpose of government. In practice, that promise competes with a political culture where loyalty to a patron counts for more than performance in office.


What impunity looks like now


The pattern shows up at every level of public life.


In politics, the Dataphyte review found that only 35 of 393 corruption defendants over 14 years were former governors, and cases against elected officials take six to fifteen years to conclude, against two to five years for appointed officials. Former Kaduna governor Nasir El-Rufai still faces a fraud charge running over hundreds of millions of naira, while opposition figures have accused the EFCC of

timing such prosecutions

 for political effect ahead of 2027. In Rivers State, repeated attempts by lawmakers aligned with FCT Minister Nyesom Wike to remove Governor Siminalayi Fubara became less a constitutional process than a political contest. Court orders, presidential intervention, and negotiated settlements repeatedly overtook legislative procedures, leaving institutional accountability secondary to political bargaining.


In public finance, the sums grow larger while accountability grows weaker. The Auditor General’s 2021 report

flagged the NNPC

 for N514 billion in unauthorised deductions and undocumented spending, and the Senate has separately been pressing NNPCL to explain N210 trillion in discrepancies across its 2017 to 2023 financial statements. BudgIT’s review of the

2025 budget

 found that lawmakers inserted 11,122 projects worth N6.93 trillion, many with no clear link to national priorities. None of these revelations has resulted in clear political consequences for those responsible.


In security, the human cost is measured in bodies, not just balance sheets. SBM Intelligence’s tracking of

kidnapping for ransom

 recorded 4,722 people abducted in 997 incidents between July 2024 and June 2025, with 762 deaths and N2.57 billion paid out against ransom demands of N48 billion. Public perception data from

Afrobarometer

 and other polls show that most Nigerians rate the police and security forces poorly in addressing crime and banditry. This judgment is reinforced by the rarity of meaningful investigations, prosecutions, or reforms following major security failures or reported abuses by state actors.


The cost of a system without …

author: Ngozi Nwosu-Juba
title: Who profits from ‘saving’ women?
content:
During a recent dialogue convened by Liberation Alliance Africa’s

Building Knowledge Bridges Community of Practice on Recentering African Feminist Epistemologies to Prevent and Respond to Sexual Violence

, bringing together activists, writers, and independent researchers from across the continent, an important and thought-provoking conversation emerged. While participants acknowledged the significant contributions of civil society organizations, development agencies, and other actors in advancing efforts to end violence against women and girls, there was also a collective reflection on the ways in which this support is framed and delivered.

I was struck by how this discussion raised critical questions about funding priorities, whose interests are ultimately served, who benefits most from existing interventions, and whether the structures and language designed to address violence may, in some instances, inadvertently reproduce inequalities or overlook the needs and voices of those most affected. The conversation challenged me to think beyond the availability of resources and examine the political, economic, and institutional dynamics that shape responses to violence against women and girls across the continent.

In my early days in feminist activism, I often highlighted to funders how our interventions had shifted away from speaking on behalf of women to “giving them voice.” This was widely regarded as progressive, even transformative, evidence that we had moved beyond paternalistic approaches and were empowering women to speak for themselves. It became a powerful narrative, one that resonated strongly with donors and development agencies alike.

Yet, over time, this language began to lose its appeal, as I started to interrogate the assumptions that underpinned it. Were women truly without voices, or were their voices simply being ignored, dismissed, or rendered unintelligible within systems of power?

The notion of “giving voice” positioned organizations like ours as benevolent intermediaries bestowing agency on those presumed to lack it. In doing so, it risked obscuring the fact that women had always spoken, resisted, negotiated, and articulated their realities, often in ways that did not fit donor expectations or development frameworks.

What does it mean to “give” women a voice? And who has the authority to bestow something that women have always possessed?

There is a long history of women’s resistance and political agency in Africa. In Nigeria, the

Women’s War of 1929

 stands as a powerful reminder that women have never been silent. Thousands of women in eastern Nigeria organized, mobilized, challenged colonial authority, and articulated their demands with remarkable courage and clarity. Their actions were neither facilitated by development projects nor enabled by donor-funded interventions. They emerged from women’s own collective consciousness, an inherited legacy of women’s determination to resist injustice.

In the Bamenda Grassfields of Northwest Cameroon, women organized one of the most significant grassroots uprisings against colonial authority in Central and West Africa. Faced with colonial policies that threatened their farmland, the women of Kom fought back.

Using

Anlu

, a traditional practice where women collectively sanction men who violate community norms, they organized marches and used satire to name and shame colonial collaborators. Through their actions, they brought administrative and economic life in the region to a standstill for months, and their protest ultimately forced the colonial government to reverse the land policies and contributed to the broader political shifts that shaped Cameroon’s path toward independence and reunification.

In Eastern Africa, Queen Muhumuza led a movement against British and German colonialists from Southern Uganda. According to the historian

Murindwa Rutanga

, Queen Muhumuza was the first major leader to mobilize peasants in Kigezi into organized anticolonial resistance against British rule starting in 1909. Drawing on her political experience and spiritual authority, she raised consciousness about the dangers of colonialism and united a broad sector of the Bakiga and neighboring communities in armed resistance. Under her leadership, communities resisted colonial boundary demarcations, obstructed missionaries and colonial agents, and challenged the expansion of colonial authority despite violent repression. Her efforts established her as one of the …

author: Simon Ramapuputla
title: Cosatu congress adjourned after credential dispute exposes tensions
content:
The Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) has adjourned its 15

th

 national congress after seven affiliates withheld their delegate credentials, preventing the federation from reaching the quorum required to proceed with the meeting.


The decision, announced after two days of difficult proceedings, brought the congress to a halt before delegates could debate the federation’s political report, organisational matters and resolutions affecting workers.


Speaking to

Elitsha

 outside the congress venue on Wednesday, Cosatu spokesperson Zanele Sabela said the decision by some affiliates not to submit their credentials was linked primarily to the suspension of Cosatu’s first deputy president, Mike Shingange, by his union, the National Education, Health and Allied Workers’ Union (Nehawu), shortly before the congress.


Sabela said the suspension had become a “bone of contention” because affiliates wanted clarity on why Shingange had been suspended on the eve of the congress and whether the move would prevent his candidacy for a leadership position. Nehawu’s general secretary clarified in the congress that the suspension was an internal union matter and did not mean Shingange could not stand for a Cosatu position. She said Shingange remained a shop steward and a member of an affiliated union.


The dispute was also taken to the Labour Court. Sabela said the court ruled on Tuesday night that the suspension did not stand, making the issue of his immediate suspension a moot point in relation to the congress.


Shingange himself told journalists that the reasons for his suspension were a matter between himself and his union. He also maintained that a person seeking a leadership position in Cosatu must meet the federation’s membership requirements.


Four Cosatu affiliates – Sadtu, Nehawu, Popcru and Sactwu – had organised a separate press conference outside of its mother body but it was later cancelled. Photo by Simon Ramapuputla


Cosatu denies clear divisions


The suspension and credential dispute unfolded alongside dissent among affiliates, with four unions calling a press briefing outside the Cosatu congress but cancelled it. Cosatu’s leadership played down the significance of the separate briefing, saying it should not be interpreted as evidence that the federation was fragmenting. They insisted disagreements among affiliates were not new and that similar tensions had been managed in previous congresses. Discussions among leaders during the two-day gathering, they argued, showed that the affiliates were not necessarily as far apart as the events at the congress suggested.


The precise reasons and positions that the four affiliates intended to advance at their separate media briefing were not fully addressed by Cosatu’s national office bearers during the federation’s own briefing. The issue was, however, part of the wider dispute about credentials, the suspension of Shingange and the conduct of the congress.


Cosatu’s leadership said seven unions attending the congress had not submitted their credential lists. Without those lists, the federation could not establish the number of eligible delegates for purposes of calculating a quorum. National office bearers said the congress spent roughly three hours dealing with the issue before the constitutional limit was reached. Under clause 3.4 of the federation’s constitution, the congress had to be adjourned and the president is required to reconvene it within 30 days.


So, the ultimate reason for the adjournment, was this technicality rather than a substantive political disagreement over the direction of the federation.


“We do not want to confirm what we cannot prove,” one of the leaders told journalists when asked whether political interests had influenced the events at the congress. The political questions that were supposed to dominate the congress included Cosatu’s relationship with the ANC and the SACP, particularly after the SACP’s decision to contest the upcoming local government elections independently.


The issue has implications for the tripartite alliance, which brings together the ANC, Cosatu and the SACP. Although the three organisations retain their decision-making processes, the ANC has long dominated its partners. During the briefing, Cosatu leaders stressed that the SACP was an independent organisation entitled to take its own decisions.


At the same time, Cosatu had been expected to debate the implications of the SACP’s electoral strategy …

author: Deogracious Kalima
title: Young Zimbabweans are being “kidnapped” and sent to rehab camps. Former detainees say they were tortured inside
content:
Former detainees say they were tortured inside.

Harare, Zimbabwe (Minority Africa) â

In the heart of Mbare Township, Harareâs poorest and most populated slum, there is a new and menacing economy emerging.

âItâs the drug trade and itâs on steroids,â says John Gwada, a community leader and pastor with the Zimbabwe Apostolic Church. Zimbabweâs youth substance abuse crisis has skyrocketed from 43% in 2017 to 57% in 2019, and is believed to be much worse today, according to the Zimbabwe Civil Liberties and Drugs Network, a monitoring agency.

This new dark-street economy is built on the broken lives of Zimbabweâs so-called âLost Generationââyoung adults born after 2000 who are the demographic most affected by the countryâs dire unemployment crisis. In 2023, researchers, citing social workers and addiction specialists, reported that 43% of school-going youths were hooked on illicit substances ranging from crystal meth (locally known as mutoriro) to tainted cough syrups and imported cocaine.

âItâs a mess, kids abandoning school, some chasing their parents out of their homes, others selling all the household furniture just to buy the next supply and feed their cravings for mutoriro,â Gwada says.

But the real horror isn't just found in the âstreet bases,â where the drugs are sold in small sachets and makeshift beer bottles. It lies behind the immaculate, steel-wire fences of so-called ârehab boot campsâ that claim to reform youths battling addictions, all for free.

Our investigation into Zimbabweâs mushrooming âdrug rehabilitationâ hubs shows that they have become a cesspool of corruption and brutality, where politically connected elites have turned a public health crisis into a money-spinning racket.

At centres such as Matrix Rehabilitation Centre, which began working around 2021/2022, and the Angel of Hope Foundation, established in Harare in 2018, former detainees and their families allege that the road to sobriety involves cash bribes, military-style torture, unlawful detention, and the disregard of basic human rights.

To a desperate parent such as Chipo Ganga*, watching her 17-year-old son waste away through mutoriro addiction, it didnât take much to fall for the sleek adverts on TikTok and Facebook promoting Zimbabweâs âdrug rehab colleges.â

âI was desperate to save my teenage son in 2025, the rehab adverts looked godsend,â she says.

The advertisements promise âholistic therapy,â âpsychological assessments,â and a path back to sanity, education, or employment for âsaved youths.â In Zimbabwe, where the formal healthcare system has all but collapsed and only 18 psychiatrists reportedly serve a population of 17 million, these seemingly non-profit rehabilitation centres pose as the only remaining hope for parents whose children are addicted to crystal meth, cocaine, illicit alcohol, or other narcotics.

The Matrix Rehabilitation Centre, owned by Tafadzwa Chidawa, a politically connected former police officer who was acquitted in March last year of an unrelated US $20,000 fraud case, and Angel of Hope, a foundation headed by Zimbabweâs First Lady, Auxillia Mnangagwa, are the most prominent of these so-called ârehab colleges.â

They claim to offer free or subsidised programmes lasting between one and three months to transform young people battling addiction into productive members of society.

But Matrixâs pitch extends beyond rehabilitation. In videos and advertisements reviewed by Minority Africa, the centre presents its programmes as a pathway to opportunities after participants leave, including education and travel abroad. Posts promote opportunities in countries including India and the United Arab Emirates, while others document participants obtaining visas and travelling overseas to study.

In one video posted in August 2026, Matrix celebrated a young woman receiving a visa to study abroad, before later chronicling her journey to India. The posts present such departures as evidence of what can follow the centreâs disciplinary programme.

Matrix has made varying claims about the success of its rehabilitation programme. In separate posts on social media, the centre has claimed success rates of 92% and 97%. The posts do not explain how Matrix defines âsuccess,â the period over which participants are followed, or what data the figures are based on.

âThe Matrix Rehabilitation Centre promised me that my 17-year-old son, who had …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Laws and Resurgent Cultural Claims: Rwanda’s Decency Policing Erodes Women’s Freedoms
content:
There’s been an online uproar after Rwandan National Police spokesperson ACP Rutikanga Boniface announced on public television that public indecency will be punished. On August 29, police officers threatened to beat young women attending a concert by Tanzanian singer Diamond Platnumz if they did not follow the new ‘decency’ orders.


In Rubavu, a town in the west of the country, a young woman was seen on video being apprehended by police over the length of her dress. Thereafter, several government workers using the X platform stated that it is important for Rwandan culture to be upheld and that the ‘Western ways’ used to sexualize women’s bodies through revealing clothing are corrupting the youth. These are not isolated incidents.


Women’s bodies and the rights of gender-expansive and marginalized people have increasingly become battlegrounds for Christian fundamentalist moralists and lobbyists.


Rwandan law does not clearly define indecency.

Article 143 of Law N° 68/2018 states: “Any person who performs an indecent act in public commits an offence.” Conviction can lead to imprisonment for six months to two years.

 In 2023, there were discussions about redefining indecency as “showing one’s private parts or performing sexual acts in public,” but this was not adopted. Ambiguity remains over what constitute

s a ‘private part,’ making enforcement unclear and subjective. This also opens the door to bias against women and girls, as body parts like shoulders or cleavage may be deemed indecent, similar to theocratic states treating exposed hair as indecent.


Social media is flooded with calls for clarity on the law, as its guidelines would be replicated at entrances to businesses, hotels, and restaurants. This demonstrates how legal ambiguity fuels public scrutiny and the policing of women and girls. Women are speaking up about how legal definitions of decency affect their lives. We cannot live in a world where a mere body can incriminate a person, or where enforcers arbitrarily decide what clothing is

 inappropriate

.


This debate is feeding into an already pervasive culture of gender-based violence whose victims are disproportionately women, girls and gender expansive people. Technology Facilitated Gender Based Violence (TFGBV), already common, is being fueled on TikTok and Instagram, where several young men and some journalists are justifying rape as the woman or girl’s fault due to what she is wearing.


On September 2, a young woman in Kibagabaga was harassed, beaten, undressed, and insulted by a group of men. The video has circulated on social media, but the perpetrators remain unpunished, and the girl’s fate is unknown. Now, online platforms—driven by manosphere communities and technocapitalists profiting from dehumanization—have become battlegrounds for controlling women’s public and private lives.


Mob violence and GBV have been normalized as of late, and public institutions have remained silent. Rwandan women and girls feel ignored, helpless, and abandoned.


The Ministry of Gender and Family Promotion, whose mandate is to champion gender equality, has in the past

 implicitly responded

to rising rates of teenage pregnancies by blaming parents and

mothers for failing to raise ‘decent’ girls

. Once again, the risk in this

rhetoric

is that women, girls, and gender-expansive people become blamed for such deeply rooted systems of inequality and oppression. Subjective matters such as manners, morals, hemline lengths, and even treating nudity as indecency are regressions rooted in colonial and religious control of African bodies.


Counting Women, Not Counting on Rights


All this is happening while women hold 64 percent of seats in parliament, yet they are not fighting against the resurgent social control of women’s bodies or the legal silences that enable it. Rwanda has had a parliamentary women’s majority for nearly two decades, yet this has not resulted in real change, as patriarchal control of women’s lives continues to resurface.


On August 7, 2022, police arrested 24-year-old Liliane Mugabekazi after a photo of her at a concert taken by a journalist circulated online. She was charged with public indecency under Article 143 and faced imprisonment. Prosecutors claimed her clothing “revealed her private parts”—her breasts. A Kicukiro Primary Court judge initially denied her bail. Mugabekazi pleaded not guilty, noting she did not take or share the photo and had passed venue security. She was later …

author: ROAPE
title: Charting the evolution of US-led imperialism, 1974-2026
content:
In 1990, Indian Marxist economist and political commentator Prabhat Patnaik asked ‘

Whatever has happened to imperialism?

’. His point was not that it had disappeared. To the contrary, he argued, “the deafening silence about imperialism is a reflection of the extraordinary strength and vigour it is displaying at present”. The silence is no more. The mask of US-led imperialism is now off. The long, drawn-out process of seeking to justify and manufacture consent for the illegal invasions of Afghanistan in 2001 and Iraq in 2003 abandoned.


In its place, bald assertions and celebrations of US imperialist intent from President Trump and his White House coterie of acolytes. The deafening explosion of US-Israeli bombs, missiles, mortars, and munitions falling from the skies over Gaza and Iran. Over

100,000 tonnes of explosives dropped on Gaza

 alone since October 2023.


Following Patnaik’s logic, this new phase of flagrant ‘might is right’ imperialism might be interpreted as a weakening of the US’ position as global imperialist hegemon. Perhaps so – yet it will not feel this way to those who suffer under its unrelenting assault.


Gaza, Iran, Venezuela and the much-less covered

intensification of the Cuban blockade

 are the most glaring examples of US-led imperialism in 2026. Who will fall next, under the pounding of US bombs, the chokehold of US sanctions or blockade, the deposing or killing of sovereign leaders?    


In such a moment, developing and deepening our understanding of US-led imperialism has become an urgent task for radical and progressive forces everywhere. In this spirit,

Review of African Political Economy

 offers a curated selection of ten open-access publications on the topic of US-led imperialism from our archives.


For the inspired reader, our

more than 50 years of easily searchable archives

 are filled with further analysis on imperialism and Africa including engagement with the broader debates concerning class, accumulation and state capture. The simple use of the keyword ‘imperialism’ alone, for instance,

returns 85 articles

 that focus in one way or another on this topic.


Collectively, the ten contributions listed below theorise the evolving drivers, manifestations and contradictions of US-led imperialism over time (for, to harness Cabral, “

nobody has yet made a successful revolution without a revolutionary theory

”) while laying bare its devastating consequences for those against whom it is directed.


US-led imperialism and Africa


1.


US imperialism and Southern Africa

, Barry Cohen (1977)


Contends Carter-era US policy toward Southern Africa sought not to end imperial domination but to manage decolonisation and racial conflict in ways that preserved  capitalist and strategic interests while containing revolutionary movements.


2.


Imperialism and the national bourgeoisie

, Bjorn Beckman (1981)


Argues local capitalist classes in postcolonial Africa are not anti-imperialist national liberators but partners of global capital, helping reproduce underdevelopment by using state power to shield both domestic and foreign elites from popular demands.


3.


Imperialism in the post-cold war era

, Giles Mohan and Alfred Zack-Williams (1995)


Demonstrates how in the post-Cold War era, imperialism has not disappeared but has been reconfigured through debt, structural adjustment, financial globalisation, and selective intervention, continuing to subordinate African development to the interests of advanced capitalist powers.


4.


Bringing imperialism back in

, Ray Bush and Morris Svfetel (1999)


Contends the dominant discourse of globalisation obscures the enduring realities of imperialism, showing how international financial institutions, debt regimes, and neoliberal restructuring deepen African dependency while presenting market rule as the only possible path to development.


5.


Africa, imperialism and new forms of accumulation

, Sarah Bracking and Graham Harrison (2003)


Argues contemporary African capitalism remains structured by imperialist relations in which global and local elites use states, markets, debt, and new forms of accumulation to reproduce inequality, exploitation, and external domination under the banner of globalisation and development.


6.


Imperialism and international governance: the case of US policy towards Africa

, Robert Biel (2003)


Shows how US policy toward Africa seeks to manage the contradictions of global capitalism through a mix of …

author: Amira El-Fekki
title: Clashes flare around Warraq with tensions high as island residents campaign for housing guarantees
content:
Warraq Island residents clashed with security forces deployed intensively on and around the Nile island this week, with tensions flaring as authorities are yet to respond to the residents’ demands for clear answers and guarantees regarding the fate of their homes and lands.


The new chapter in talks between residents and authorities comes as families in Warraq take action to disrupt the government’s ongoing development project and seek firm guarantees that officials will support them to stay in their homes and lands.


Security forces set up on Tuesday metal mesh barriers at the entrance to the Qolaly ferry crossing that connects the island to the Nile bank, and, on Wednesday, more barriers were added in the vicinity of the crossing, according to a resident of the island who spoke to Mada Masr.


The measures, they said, add to a series of existing restrictions already imposed on the residents’ movement and access to key goods and services.


The new barriers appear intended to protect security personnel, after stones were thrown during clashes with residents near the ferry crossing in the preceding days, the resident said.


The latest of these took place at Qolaly on Sunday and Monday, with several residents injured as a result, including a young man whose skull was fractured in the clashes, they added.


To protest the security response to the Qolaly clashes, several residents also gathered at a demonstration on Monday evening near a security forces deployment stationed beneath the Tahya Misr Bridge that runs through the island.


The gathering ended in further

clashes

, according to two residents who were present. The confrontations were visible in footage posted by Warraq residents on social media.


As the ban on construction materials entering the island continues, the Qolaly ferry crossing, the main entry point to Warraq from Giza, has been a flashpoint of near-daily confrontations between residents and security forces for around nine years. One resident said to Mada Masr that the friction around the entry of materials to the island arises mainly between security forces and residents who work to deliver construction supplies to the island — but the clashes it triggers spill over to other residents in the area around the ferry.


The clashes come in parallel to a campaign to remain the island that residents have pursued since August. A large number of island residents have begun organizing as part of a group called Staying on Warraq, pushing for firm guarantees from authorities regarding the fate of their land and homes, according to several residents who have spoken to Mada Masr in recent weeks, particularly as circulating reports and unofficial maps of the government’s development project appear to include parts of the residents’ lands.


For years, residents have watched the development project unfold, waiting to learn what would happen to them, while their access to basic services on the island — like healthcare and education — has deteriorated due to state restrictions, leaving residents to establish replacements or alternatives themselves. Their efforts have included spending around LE400,000 to prepare schools for the current academic year.


They have now concluded that waiting has brought no solutions, as the state continues to carry out the project after

acquiring

most of the island’s land, the residents have said.


As part of this campaign, residents attempted on Sunday to obstruct the state’s road construction work on the island, blocking the way of transportation trucks involved in the state development project. The following day, they

held

a protest outside the New Warraq City Development Authority, where they vowed to escalate until their demands are met.


“People went out and stood outside the authority because the state is now building the roads, and they found out that the roads are getting close to residents’ homes. What impact will this have in terms of demolitions?” a lawyer from the island told Mada Masr.


“The state doesn’t solve anything. It wants to suffocate people so that they get fed up and leave,” one of the two residents who witnessed Monday’s clashes said. They said residents planned to continue disrupting the construction work being carried out by the state. “God willing, all the work will stop,” they said.


The second resident said halting construction has an impact that “is felt quickly” because the work involves multiple companies and bodies. Clashes, by contrast …

author: Nodjigno Pierre Yao Nihtael
title: What Togo’s Music Industry Needs Beyond Streaming
content:
Over the past few years, access to digital music platforms has changed what is possible for artists in countries such as Togo. A musician no longer needs to be based in Paris, London, Lagos or Johannesburg to place a release on Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube and other international services. In theory, the distance between a young artist in Lomé and a global audience has become much smaller. But access to streaming platforms is only the beginning. Distribution is not the same thing as career development, and uploading a song is not the same thing as building a sustainable music business.


Through my work in digital distribution and artist development in Togo, including projects involving more than 50 artists, I have repeatedly seen the same challenge: talent is present, ambition is present and digital access is improving, but the professional infrastructure around the artist is still developing.


For many emerging artists, the first question is how to get a song online. The more important questions come afterwards. Is the release properly prepared? Is the metadata accurate? Is the artist’s identity consistent across platforms? Is there a realistic release strategy? Are the rights and credits clearly documented? Is there a media plan? Is anyone studying the data after release and using it to make the next decision?


The author working across different devices to produce music from Togo and the continent.


These details may appear technical, but they can determine whether an artist builds a catalogue and a career or simply releases songs that disappear into an enormous digital marketplace. This is why smaller African music markets need to think beyond streaming. The next stage is infrastructure.


First, artists need stronger professional preparation before release. A good song should arrive on digital platforms as part of a structured project, with correct information, artwork, credits, promotional assets and a clear timetable. Too often, the marketing conversation begins only after a song has already been released.


Second, artist development and management need greater attention. Many talented musicians are expected to become performers, managers, marketers, content creators and business administrators at the same time. That is difficult even in mature music industries. Developing more managers, distributors, media professionals, booking agents and project coordinators around artists can create stronger careers and reduce the pressure on musicians to do everything alone.


Third, local and regional media remain important. Global platforms can distribute music internationally, but audiences still need stories, context and trusted cultural voices. Strong African music journalism can help document careers, explain new movements and connect artists to audiences beyond short social-media trends. Media visibility should not be treated simply as promotion; it is also part of building a documented cultural history.


Fourth, Togo can benefit from deeper regional connections. Our market should not be viewed in isolation. There are natural cultural and commercial links with Ghana, Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Burkina Faso, Nigeria and other West African countries. Collaborations between artists are useful, but collaborations between managers, distributors, media organisations, event producers and other professionals can be just as important.


Finally, the industry needs more education around rights, data and long-term planning. Digital platforms generate information about where listeners are located, which songs are being discovered and how audiences respond. Used correctly, this information can guide touring, promotion, collaborations and future releases. At the same time, artists need a better understanding of ownership, credits and the administrative side of their work.


Togo does not need to copy another country’s music industry exactly. Its ecosystem can develop according to its own realities, languages, cultural traditions and market size. But some principles are universal: artists need professional teams, reliable information, strong networks, good documentation and strategies that continue beyond the day a song is uploaded. Streaming has opened an important door. The challenge now is to build the structure that allows more artists to walk through that door and


remain in the industry for the long term.


That is where I believe the next phase of Togo’s music economy will be decided: not only on the platforms …

author: Gary Chartier
title: Memetakan Libertarianisme Kiri: Sebuah Tinjauan Awal
content:
Oleh:

Gary Chartier

. Teks aslinya berjudul “

Framing Left Libertarianism: A First Pass

”. Diterjemahkan ke Bahasa Indonesia oleh Taratsa.


Libertarianisme kiri (

left libertarianism

, selanjutnya LL) dapat dipandang sebagai sekadar upaya mengemas gagasan dan membangun propaganda. Namun, ia juga dapat dipahami sebagai ekspresi kuat dari berbagai persoalan yang semestinya menjadi inti dari gerakan-gerakan kebebasan.


Kaum libertarian maupun kelompok kiri yang sinis mungkin sama-sama melihat pembicaraan mengenai LL sebagai permainan retorika. Bisa jadi, mereka menganggapnya sebagai upaya untuk menjual gagasan-gagasan libertarian kepada orang-orang kiri naif yang tidak menyadari bahwa gagasan tersebut pada dasarnya bertentangan dengan agenda politik kiri. Atau sebaliknya, mungkin LL dipandang sebagai upaya mencangkokkan sesuatu yang asing ke dalam tubuh gerakan libertarian, membebaninya dengan berbagai persoalan yang dianggap tidak memiliki tempat dalam agenda libertarian yang sesungguhnya.


Kedua pandangan tersebut sama-sama tidak meyakinkan dan tidak menarik.


LL benar-benar libertarian karena ia

anti-negara

—para libertarian kiri yang langsung terlintas dalam pikiran saya semuanya adalah anarkis; dalam tulisan ini saya menganggap bahwa seorang libertarian kiri adalah seorang anarkis, atau setidaknya cukup dekat dengan anarkisme sehingga perbedaannya tidak relevan—dan karena ia mengakui nilai pasar serta hak kepemilikan. Pada saat yang sama, LL juga benar-benar berhaluan kiri karena berupaya menantang privilese, hierarki, eksklusi, deprivasi, dan dominasi, baik secara ideologis maupun praktis, serta dapat menunjukkan komitmen yang sungguh-sungguh terhadap inklusi, pemberdayaan, dan saling menghormati.


Dan semua itu dapat dilakukan bukan dengan mendefinisikan ulang berbagai istilah—misalnya dengan mengatakan bahwa kebebasan dari paksaan fisik adalah satu-satunya bentuk kebebasan yang benar-benar penting—melainkan dengan menunjukkan

keselarasan

 antara cita-cita dan prinsip libertarian dengan penerimaan yang sungguh-sungguh terhadap persoalan-persoalan utama yang menjadi perhatian gerakan kiri.


Hal itu dapat dilakukan dengan menunjukkan implikasi radikal dari prinsip-prinsip libertarian yang selama ini telah diterima secara luas.


• Misalnya, dapat ditunjukkan bahwa sejarah kekerasan dan kolusi dengan— atau bahkan dukungan terhadap— tirani yang dilakukan oleh individu dan organisasi yang memiliki kekuatan ekonomi telah merusak legitimasi hak kepemilikan yang mereka pegang, sekaligus memberikan dasar bagi

penguasaan melalui

homesteading

 atas apa yang mereka klaim sebagai properti oleh orang-orang yang hidup dan bekerja di atasnya

.


• Demikian pula, penerapan penuh prinsip-prinsip libertarian mengenai ketidakadilan dan dampak buruk monopoli serta subsidi kemungkinan besar akan melemahkan, dalam berbagai cara, kekuasaan organisasi bisnis yang hierarkis dan tersentralisasi. Hal itu juga dapat mempermudah penggantian banyak perusahaan tersebut dengan koperasi yang dikelola oleh pekerja, sekaligus secara drastis meningkatkan pengaruh pekerja dalam sebagian besar perusahaan lainnya.


• Prinsip-prinsip libertarian yang sama juga dapat digunakan untuk menolak bentuk privilese yang memungkinkan perusahaan, kelompok profesi, dan individu yang memiliki pengaruh menggunakan kekuasaan negara untuk mengeksploitasi orang lain. Misalnya, perusahaan yang memiliki koneksi politik dapat memperoleh keistimewaan perpajakan yang memberi mereka keuntungan non-pasar atas para pesaingnya. Demikian pula, kelompok profesi tertentu dapat merugikan masyarakat sekaligus calon pesaing dari kalangan miskin dengan mempertahankan kekayaan dan privilese melalui persyaratan lisensi yang mahal, yang diberlakukan atau dipertahankan atas tekanan mereka melalui negara.


• Dan prinsip yang sama yang mengutuk negara secara umum juga memberikan dasar yang kuat untuk menentang perang dan imperialisme secara khusus.


LL juga dapat menekankan sejauh mana

prinsip-prinsip moral yang sama

 yang mendorong penolakan terhadap kekuasaan negara yang menindas dapat menjadi alasan kuat untuk menantang berbagai ketimpangan sosial yang secara tepat telah menjadi perhatian banyak orang di kalangan kiri. Sejauh penolakan terhadap kekuasaan negara berakar pada teori moral tertentu, apa pun bentuknya, teori tersebut dapat digunakan untuk menghasilkan penilaian moral mengenai persoalan-persoalan di luar kekuasaan negara. author: APTN National News
title: Feds ask Court to overturn Tribunal decision on commissioners overseeing child welfare case
content:
Canada’s justice ministry is requesting a Federal Court review a decision by the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal not to fill positions on the commission overseeing the reform of the First Nation child welfare system and Jordan’s Principle program.


The move is in response to an Aug. 18 decision by Tribunal chair Jennifer Khurana to not appoint two new commissioners to the case that has languished for nearly 15 years.


In July, the federal government requested that Khurara add the commissioners because when the Tribunal started hearing the case in 2012, the panel consisted of members Sophie Marchildon, Réjean Bélanger and Edward Lustig. Bélanger died suddenly in 2015, leaving just two to oversee the case. 

Lustig resigned on July 7,

 leaving just Marchildon.


According to the government, the case has gotten more complex since Bélanger’s death and requested that the chair not allow Marchildon to continue on her own.


Parties, including the Assembly of First Nations and the First Nations Child and Family Caring Society, argued having to bring new commissioners up to speed would delay the hearings.


Khurana agreed with the parties.


“The Chairperson has reviewed the parties’ submissions in response to the AGC’s panel recomposition,” wrote a short reply from chair Khurana and released by the registrar. “The AGC’s [Attorney General of Canada] request is dismissed.


According to the chair, reasons she dismissed the request will follow.


In its application to the Federal Court, the government argues that the Tribunal’s decision was not “rational and logical” and that it “failed to consider the evidence and submissions before it.”


“Given the history of the underlying matter, the number of parties and interested participants involved, and the complexity of the issues raised, the Attorney General of Canada is of the view that case management is necessary to ensure the effective management and expeditious disposition of this proceeding,” the justice department letter said.


In 2016, the Tribunal ruled that Canada discriminated against First Nations children by knowingly underfunding programs that were supposed to help them. They ordered the discrimination to end immediately and that all sides work together to come up with a plan to reform the system.


A decade later, Marchildon is now reviewing plans put forward by the federal government and another by a group called the National Children’s Chiefs’ Commission – a body commissioned by chiefs across the country.

Feds ask Court to overturn Tribunal decision on commissioners overseeing child welfare case

APTN News
