author: groundxero
title: Sugar Prices Soar, Mill Profits Swell, Farmers Demands Share in the Surplus
content:
As sugar prices surge from Rs 48.18 to Rs 62 per kg in less than two months, SKM – the joint platform of farmers’ unions

 –

accuses Modi government of facilitating market profiteering; demands Rs 5,500 per tonne for raw cane and mandatory sharing of sugar-industry surplus with cane farmers

.


 


Groundxero Desk


Sep 17, 2026


 


The Samyukta Kisan Morcha (SKM) has accused the BJP-led Narendra Modi government of facilitating “market loot of people” through what it describes as an “unbridled” and unjustifiable surge in retail sugar prices, while allowing sugar mills, traders and the politically poweful sugar lobby to amass huge profits by looting farmers as well as consumers.


 


In a press note issued in New Delhi on September 17, the joint platform of farmers’ unions, pointed to the sharp rise in retail sugar prices over the past two months. According to SKM, sugar was selling at an average retail price of Rs 48.18 per kg on July 20, 2026. The price rose to Rs 55.70 on August 20, Rs 58.23 on August 21 and Rs 62 on September 15. In several markets, it has reportedly crossed Rs 70 per kg.


 


SKM has demanded that the government to end its surrender to the powerful sugar mill lobby and urgently intervene to curb speculative trading and regulate sugar prices. Its principal demands include fixing the sugarcane price at Rs 5,500 per tonne, and enacting a law mandating the sharing of sugar mills’ surplus with cane farmers.


 


Sugar mills, ethanol and the politics of surplus appropriation


 


SKM has linked the current sugar price rise to the increasing diversion of sugarcane towards ethanol production. Average sugar production between 2020-21 and 2025-26 has remained around 32–34 million tonnes, while the quantity of sugarcane diverted for ethanol has increased substantially in recent years.


 


According to SKM, the quantity of sugar diverted for ethanol production rose from five lakh metric tonnes, or 2 per cent, in 2018-19 to 22 lakh metric tonnes, or 6 per cent, in 2020-21, and 43 lakh metric tonnes, or 13 per cent, in 2022-23. With cane production declining, the figure fell to 34 lakh metric tonnes, or 10.5 per cent, in 2024-25.


 


The organisation argues that the policy has created conditions in which sugar mills and wholesale traders benefit from high ethanol and sugar prices, while cane farmers see little corresponding gain.


 


SKM has presented an example of the estimated loot by sugar mills based on a standard medium-to-large private sugar mill in Uttar Pradesh with a crushing capacity of approximately 5,000–8,000 tonnes of cane per day. Assuming a 130–150-day crushing season, it estimates annual white-sugar production at around 80,000 tonnes, with a commercial recovery rate of 10 per cent after molasses separation.


 


At the current premium State Advised Price (SAP) of Rs 395 per quintal, SKM estimates the annual cost of raw sugarcane for such a mill at around Rs 316 crore. Adding an estimated Rs 48 crore in operational costs—including labour, chemicals, packaging, maintenance and field logistics—the total annual expenditure is put at approximately Rs 364 crore or Rs 600 per tonne.


 


Against this, using the ex-factory sugar prices recorded in August 2026, SKM estimates the mill’s annual turnover from white commercial sugar at Rs 432 crore and total gross revenue, including molasses, bagasse and pressmud, at Rs 551.76 crore. It puts the estimated net profit at Rs 187.76 crore.


 


At an ex-factory sugar price of Rs 48 per kg, SKM estimates the annual net profit of such a standard Uttar Pradesh sugar mill at Rs 139.76 crore annually.


 


SKM argues that if 50 per cent of this profit were shared with cane producing farmers, the cane price could rise by approximately Rs 873.50 per tonne, taking it to around Rs 4,820 per tonne.


 


The figures are presented by SKM as an illustration of the distribution of surplus in the sugar industry, rather than as an audited industry-wide calculation.


 


Cane farmers squeezed at both ends


Farmers grow the cane. Consumers buy the sugar. Yet, the mills and traders, SKM alleges, pocket the expanding surplus. As retail sugar surges the Modi government is protecting the interests of the sugar mill owners while leaving farmers squeezed between rising input costs and stagnant cane prices. SKM is demanding Rs 5,500 per tonne for sugarcane and a law mandating that sugar mills share their surplus with the farmers who produce their raw material …

author: John David Parol
title: US bases noon, Pax Silica ngayon; kabataan, nagprotesta kontra panghihimasok ng US
content:
Nagsagawa ng kilos-protesta ang iba’t ibang grupo ng mga kabataang estudyante mula sa UP Manila patungong US Embassy upang gunitain ang makasaysayang desisyon ng Senado ng Pilipinas na tanggihan ang renewal ng US Military Bases Agreement (MBA) at ratipikasyon ng RP-U.S. Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation, and Security noong 1991.

Bitbit nila ang samu’t saring panawagan kabilang ang pagbasura sa Pax Silica, pagbuwag sa Luzon Economic Corridor, at pagpapalayas sa mga tropang Amerikano at kanilang mga base-militar sa bansa sa ilalim ng Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA).

Bagamat hindi nakalapit sa mismong tarangkahan ng embahada ang mga nagpoprotesta, ipinagpatuloy ng grupo ang kanilang maikling programa sa Kalaw Avenue sa Maynila.

Ayon sa mga nagprotesta, hindi hiwalay sa pang-araw-araw na kalagayan ng mamamayan at kabataan sa Metro Manila ang krisis dulot ng patuloy na pagyuko at pagsuko ng administrasyong Marcos Jr. ng soberanya sa malalaking dayuhan tulad ng US. Anila, sa halip na tunay na pambansang industriyalisasyon, nagpapatuloy ang banta sa likas-yaman at batayang serbisyo gaya ng kuryente at tubig na lalong magpapabigat sa gastusin ng ordinaryong pamilya.

“Ngayon pa lang, sobrang taas na ng singil sa kuryente. What more kung magkakaroon ng Pax Silica? Tayo ang magbabayad ng kuryente na ginagamit ng US,” diin ni Carla Espera mula sa Liga ng mga Kabataang Propagandista (LKP).

Kinakailangang mag-supply ng 3 Gigawatt (GW) na kuryente para gumana ang itatayong industrial at manufacturing hub sa ilalim ng Pax Silica Initiative. Katumbas ito ng 16% kabuuang current grid capacity ng Luzon. Ani Espera, hindi na nga natutugunan ng gobyerno ang pangangailangan at mas murang kuryente para sa mamamayan, may pangamba pang balikatin ng mamamayan ang posibleng kasalatan sa kuryente o mataas na singil sa kuryente kaugnay sa pagpapatayo at pagpapagana sa Pax Silica.

Bahagi rin sa isinusulong ng administrasyong Marcos Jr. ang nuclear energy at liquefied natural gas (LNG) upang tugunan ang lumalaking pangangailangan sa kuryente. Gayunman, ang pagpapalawak ng mga energy at industrial infrastructure ay may usapin din sa paggamit ng lupa. Sa ilalim ng Special Economic Zone Act o Republic Act No. 7916, maaaring ma-convert ang agricultural lands para sa ilang industrial at economic-zone developments, habang may mga probisyon para sa compensation sa mga residenteng maaaring ma-displace.

Pinalawig naman ni Zamann Milagrosa ng Kabataan Partylist (KPL) ang epekto ng Pax Silica sa New Clark City sa Tarlac, na siyang sentro ng proyektong digital sa ilalim ng Luzon Economic Corridor na nagdurugtong mula Subic, Clark, Maynila, hanggang Batangas.

“Hindi dahil malayo ang (Metro Manila) sa Tarlac, ay hindi na tayo maaapektuhan, kasi connected siya sa Luzon Economic Corridor. Papunta siya sa Pax Silica, marami tayong proyekto na patungo sa Pax Silica, may ginagawang highway na maapektuhan yung pagputol ng puno at malakihang pagputol ng puno, at yung mga tubigan natin na mawawalan tayo ng malinis na tubigan,” ani Milagrosa.

Noong 2024, naglatag ang National Economic and Development Authority ng 21 proyektong isinasaalang-alang sa pagtataguyod ng LEC. Aabot sa trilyong piso ang halaga ng mga proyektong ito. Lima sa mga ito ang may direktang koneksyon sa Metro Manila. Kabilang dito ang North-South Commuter Railway, Laguna Lakeshore Road Network, North Luzon East Expressway, Manila Bay–Pasig River–Laguna Lake Ferry System, at ang Subic-Clark-Manila-Batangas Railway.

“’Yong mga magsasaka natin mawawalan ng tirahan at papalayasin sila sa lupang ninuno nila. Imbes na ‘yung tubig na napupunta sa irigasyon—dahil magkakaroon pa tayo ng super El Niño, mawawalan sila ng malinis na tubig. ‘Yong kuryente na dapat napupunta sa mga taong bayan sa Gitnang Luzon, sobrang laki ang mapupunta sa Pax Silica. Tatlong gigawatts ang kukunin nila,” dagdag pa ni Milagrosa.

Bukod sa banta sa kabuhayan ng mga katutubo at magsasaka, iginiit ng mga nagpoprotesta na ang panghihimasok ng US sa bansa sa pamamagitan LEC, Pax Silica at iba pang mga hindi pantay na kasunduan ay tahasang naglalagay sa Pilipinas sa umiigting na girian ng mga makapangyarihang bansa, partikular ang US at Tsina sa rehiyon.

“Gagamitin ang Pax Silica bilang pagawaan ng materyales pandigmaan. Ibig sabihin, gagamitin tayo bilang base ng US para madali na silang makapag-atake ng karatig-bansa na umaatake sa kanila. Kumbaga, gagawin tayong base for war dahil nandito sa atin ang siyam na …

author: Brian Hioe
title: Will the National Contact Point System Help Resolve Wrongdoing by Taiwanese Companies Abroad?
content:
AT THE START of this month, Taiwanese and Indonesian groups submitted the first complaint to the Ministry of Economic Affairs (MOEA) under the new National Contact Point (NCP) complaint system. As the name implies, the system designates the MOEA as the place where complaints about wrongdoings by Taiwanese companies internationally should be directed. Nevertheless, the Taiwanese government was criticized for announcing that the MOEA would serve as Taiwan’s NCP in September 2024, but delaying its actual rollout.

A number of criticisms from Indonesian groups centered around Taiwanese companies in the environmentally destructive nickel mining industry. Among the groups present were Action for Ecology and People Emancipation, the FSPIM Morowali Labour Union, as well as Fagawene, a local organization based out of the Weda Bay Area.

Nickel mining is a highly carbon-intensive endeavor, and it is reliant on coal-burning power plants. In addition to air pollution, wastewater discharge has led to coral deaths. This has damaged fishing grounds, killed coral reefs, and impacted river and lake ecosystems in Sagea. Tourist sites such as the Boki Maruru Cave have also been put at risk of irreversible damage. Deforestation affects residential areas, worsening issues of flooding while depriving local communities of access to clean water.

Likewise, safety practices were criticized as lacking for workers. Apart from dangerous accidents, workers have not been provided with dust collection equipment and personal protective gear, even in smelting facilities. Furthermore, facilities are poorly ventilated.

The Taiwanese government was called on to comply with international mechanisms in accepting the complaint, as well as implementing the NCP system. The Taiwanese civil society groups present, which included the Taiwan Association for Human Rights and Taiwan Labour Front, suggested that a failure to take action would worsen Taiwan’s international image. The MOEA was criticized, however, for still failing to disclose the details of the complaint review process, as well as for delays in releasing the National Action Plan on Business and Human Rights at a time when Taiwanese companies such as Giant Bicycle have fallen afoul of a Withhold Release Order in the US over forced labor allegations.

In this sense, Taiwanese companies and the government were called on to undertake responsible corporate diligence in line with international standards. But it may not be surprising if one continues to see the government continue to drag its feet, acting to defend corporate interests instead of calling them to account.

author: rti_admin
title: Bablai Mata Yatra: How Does Development Politics Affect Madia Culture?
content:
For the Madia Adivasi community in the Bhamragad region, the Bablai Mata Yatra (pilgrimage/fair) is not just a religious pilgrimage but a living symbol of cultural, environmental, and constitutional rights.

However, in recent times, the politics of development, religious conversion, the administration, and Naxalism have begun to significantly impact the Bablai Yatra.

For the Madia Adivasi community in the Bhamragad area, the Bablai Mata Yatra is not merely a religious fair but a living symbol of their cultural, environmental, and constitutional rights. Every year, thousands of Madia Adivasi people from the Bhamragad tract come together to worship Bablai Mata and to renew their generations-old culture, traditions, and relationship with nature. Yet, in the name of development, the pilgrimage of Bablai Devi is slowly disappearing.

According to Adivasi tradition, Bablai was the sister of a man named Morka. Bablai was married to Thakur Dev, who is still worshipped at a shrine on Surjagad today. After their marriage, Thakur Dev went to Surjagad for a second wife, but Bablai did not go away with her people. She stayed in this region, remained among the people here, and became one with this land and forest.

The locals say that their faith was born from this sacrifice:

She left her husband for us, but she never left us, and that is why she is a goddess for us.

Today, Bablai Mata is the presiding deity of Adivasis across the Bhamragad region. This story is not found in written form, but this tradition has been carried forward from generation to generation through the words of the ancestors.

Traditional Governance: Bhoom Perma, Bhoomiya, and Kathdi

The Bablai Yatra is not only about worshipping the deity; it is also where the traditional self-governance system of the Adivasis becomes visible. The highest position in this system is “Bhoom Perma” (in simple terms, the “President” of this traditional system). The Bhoomiya (or Bhoom Bhoomiya) is considered the owner and protector of that place. There are also traditional office bearers like Bhoom, Kotwal, and Kathdi (village-level customary officials). This group consists of around 22 members and includes active participation of women. Together, they handle the worship of Bablai Mata, management of the Yatra, decision-making processes, and the entire religious and cultural programme. In essence, this structure is the local expression of the gram sabha (village assembly), self-governance, and collective decision-making. The Adivasi community believes that Bablai Mata protects all the water, forests, and land in the region. Therefore, the central focus of the Yatra is not only religious rituals but a spiritual relationship with nature.

People from many villages in the Bhamragad area come together to clean the sacred groves in the forest, consider trees, water bodies, and hills as deities, and follow a code of conduct that ensures no harm to nature.

Law, Constitution, and Cultural Protection

Before 2013, the Bablai festival was not celebrated in this form. Even after Independence, the influence of the princely state remained here. After India became independent, the kings of the Aheri State used to visit this tract. People here worshipped them like Brahma Dev — falling at their feet, washing their feet, and serving them through performances like dancing by women performers. The kings would come once or twice a year and enjoy such festivities. This practice continued until about fifteen to twenty years ago. People used to come to Bejur village only for Bablai Mata’s darshan (sacred viewing/audience with the deity).

Later, local scholar-youth took the initiative and made people aware that before Independence they were subjects of the British, and that after Independence the Constitution abolished the princely order. They formed a traditional Kuthul committee (customary coordinating body) in the Bhamragad belt and, by bringing all gram sabhas together, decided that they would gather right here and organise Bablai Mata’s traditional worship and a traditional convention in a proper way. Along with this, all the gram sabhas in the Bhamragad area began discussing the Forest Rights Act and PESA. The Yatra thus became not only a cultural symbol for the Madia community but also a space for public awareness.

author: Rojava IC
title: Sleeper-Cell Report July 2026 – Global Coalition reports 0 confirmed ISIS attacks
content:
An ISIS flag was raised on a school building in al-Zubari, eastern Deir ez-Zor countryside


 


Key Points


– Six sleeper-cell attacks recorded by RIC, but the Global Coalition claims 0 attacks were officially claimed by ISIS


– One military personnel was killed, and a further five injured


– A minimum of seven alleged ISIS members were arrested


– A total of 36 civilians were injured, two killed


– An ISIS flag was raised on a school building in Deir ez-Zor


–

Two Tunisian families linked to ISIS mercenaries repatriated from Roj camp


 


In-Depth


In July of 2026, RIC

recorded six sleeper-cell attacks which some publications have attributed to ISIS, according to


North Press Agency

 one of these attacks was claimed by ISIS whereas the


Global Coalition


reported that July was the first month since the territorial defeat of ISIS in 2019, where they claimed 0 attacks. Also this month at least 7 members of ISIS cells were arrested.


On July 7, Bombings struck central Damascus near the Ministry of Tourism and the Four Seasons Hotel, during the visit of Macron the president of France to Syria. Ministry of Interior has attributed the attack to ISIS, the bombing resulted in the killing of one civilian and injury of 36.


On July 8, three attacks happened during the same day and the are believed to have been carried out by ISIS members.

Unidentified gunmen on a motorcycle used machine guns to target an oil truck in Abrahyah town in eastern Deir ez-Zor countryside, killing the driver.


Similarly, unidentified gunmen on a motorcycle, attacked a checkpoint of the Internal Security Forces near al-Baserah city bridge.


According to North Press Agency, also on July 8 ISIS

claimed responsibility for the killing of Rashad Khalaf al-Ghurair in the northern countryside of Deir ez-Zor.


On July 15,

unknown gunmen on a motorcycle opened fire on a member of the 72nd Division on the road linking al-Arimah and Manbij in eastern Aleppo countryside, injuring the him.


On July 18,

two unidentified gunmen on a motorcycle opened fire directly on member of the Defence Ministry


near al-Awsajli junction in eastern Manbij city.


On July 9,

Syria’s Interior Ministry announced its security forces had dismantled several ISIS cells in southern Syria, arresting a senior leader and several members accused of involvement in assassinations and financing terror.


On July 28,

Syrian Internal Security Forces and the General Intelligence Service in Aleppo announced the arrest of individuals allegedly affiliated with the ISIS, during a security operation in Aleppo and its surrounding countryside.


An ISIS flag was raised on a school building in al-Zubari, eastern Deir ez-Zor countryside, in an incident that sparked widespread concern among residents.


During July, Two Tunisian families linked to ISIS were repatriated from


Roj Camp, which houses families of ISIS members, and returned to Tunisia. Additionally, Tunisian citizen Bilal Chawachi was sentenced to 55 years in prison after being convicted on terrorism-related charges, specifically traveling to Syria and fighting alongside the extremist organization.


Germany sentenced an Iraqi man to life imprisonment and his former wife to nine years and six months in prison after convicting them of enslaving and torturing two Yazidi girls while they were members of ISIS in Syria and Iraq between 2015 and 2017.


Three U.S. citizens pleaded guilty to terror charges, prosecutors said the defendants communicated through encrypted messaging applications between July and November 2025 and planned to travel to Turkey before crossing into Syria to join ISIS. 


* Due to the low rate of confirmed ISIS attacks RIC has decided to stop publishing monthly sleeper-cell reports and instead share a bi-annual summary of ISIS activity throughout Syria.

title: Bayık: As long as Öcalan is not physically freed, the state’s law will not be implemented
content:
In an extensive interview with NÛÇE TV’s Hevpeyvîn program, Cemil Bayik, co-chair of the KCK (Kurdistan Communities Union) Executive Council, answered a wide variety of questions regarding the progress of the Peace and Democratic Society Process in Turkey, as well as developments in the region. Bayik particularly emphasized the crucial role played by the situation of the Kurdish people’s leader, Abdullah Öcalan, and offered insights into various aspects of the struggle.


What stage is the Peace and Democratic Society Process at?


The law passed by the Turkish Parliament does not meet our demands. The Turkish state enacted this law not in accordance with our demands, but rather in line with its own interests. The primary purpose of this law is the disarmament and disbandment of the guerrillas. Some articles have been included in the law that are not very important from our perspective. This is their law; we have our own laws as well. Neither their laws nor our laws are being enforced. There is a struggle between us and the Turkish state over this law.


What is important to us is ensuring that the necessary conditions and circumstances are in place for Rêber Apo [Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan] to carry out this process and bring it to a successful conclusion. This newly enacted law contains no principles regarding the resolution of the Kurdish issue. Rêber Apo wants the Kurdish issue to be resolved at the negotiating table. Bahçeli made some assessments in this regard. This was and is important in terms of giving the issue official recognition. This is important to us. If they clear the way for Rêber Apo and provide him with the opportunity to work freely, he can bring this process to a successful conclusion.


Were your views sought before the law was submitted to parliament?


Rêber Apo does not take any steps without us. He seeks our views. We may not be holding direct talks with the Turkish state or Imrali, but we find our ways to convey our views to Rêber Apo. When Rêber Apo wishes to take a step, he takes our decisions and views into account. Messages are sent and received through the delegation of the DEM Party. Rêber Apo did not make the decision to dissolve the PKK as a result of a meeting with the Turkish state – he took this step of his own volition. Rêber Apo trusts himself, his movement, and his people. He has no other guarantee beyond this.


Will the state take any steps regarding the Kurdish issue?


Just as the state acts in its own interests, we and our people also have our own interests. The law can act as a foundation. We can work on this basis and achieve certain results. If democracy does not advance in Turkey, the Kurdish issue will not be resolved. But still, our movement and Rêber Apo view this law as insufficient. We are taking steps with a patient, conscious, and strategic approach. Kurds are a force in the Middle East. Certain powers want to use this force for their own interests. However, we want to put this power at the service of the Kurdish people.


Amid the developments taking place in the world, will the Kurdish issue be resolved?


When the Third World War began in the Middle East, the Kurdish issue came to the forefront. The time and conditions for resolving the Kurdish issue have been created. What happens next depends on Kurdish unity. Resolving the Kurdish issue is possible only through Kurdish unity.


Did the state ask you to visit Imrali?


Certain efforts were made before the framework law reached Parliament. Rêber Apo, in particular, spearheaded these efforts. Rather than just talking, practical steps need to be taken in the political and legal spheres. Journalists and advisors have to be able to travel there to meet with Rêber Apo. Politicians and academics also need to be enabled to go to Imrali. This needs to happen in the near future. There is a great deal of skepticism in both the Kurdish and Turkish societies. Rêber Apo’s address dispels these doubts. Turkey’s approach also creates doubts among us. The KCK also needs to visit Imrali, and we will go to Imrali. This step is necessary for Turkey more than for the Kurds. Because the Turkish state is in a bad situation. The war being waged around the world is putting Turkey in a very difficult position. Turkey wanted to defeat the PKK using all the means at its disposal, but it failed to achieve this goal.


Is there direct communication between you and Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan?

author: Sarah Raymundo
title: Blood Rush | $100 barrel, super El Niño and Pax Silica: Energy hegemony, enclosure, and national liberation
content:
The AI-assisted illustration of the proposed 1,600-hectare industrial hub to be located in New Clark City in Capas, Tarlac. Photo courtesy of the People’s Television Network

The convergence of crude oil surpassing $100 per barrel and the acceleration of El Niño to “super” status—drawn from projections and reports by energy-market analysts, international economic-monitoring bodies, and climate agencies tracking compound global shocks—exposes the deep structural crisis of monopoly capitalism. This dual rupture demonstrates how imperialist war-making, extractive plunder, planetary warming, and the ongoing enclosure of the countryside function not as separate phenomena, but as interconnected expressions of the same underlying logic of capital accumulation.

The rapid climb of crude oil past $100 per barrel cannot be detached from the escalation of U.S.-led imperialist aggression, military blockades, and regional destabilization. Financialized markets and transnational fossil-fuel monopolies exploit war and artificial scarcity to protect superprofits, while the resulting inflation functions as a mechanism of structural extraction from working classes in colonies and semicolonies. Peripheral societies are forced to absorb the crisis through debt traps, budget cuts, declining purchasing power, and reduced national sovereignty. High energy prices further incentivize ruling elites to expand speculative and destructive extraction projects in the name of energy security and geopolitical hegemony.

This energy regime is increasingly bound up with “Pax Silica”—the global alliance centered on microelectronics, semiconductor supply chains, and automated defense systems. Localized military interventions rely on a global network of critical mineral extraction, energy consumption, and defense technology transfer. The fusion of high-tech militarism and fossil capital reinforces imperialist control over global supply lines, shifting the operational costs of planetary warfare directly onto the working classes of the Global South.

At the same time, a “super” El Niño brings the violence of ecological crisis directly to the doorsteps of the global peasantry, smallholders, and urban poor. Although the historical carbon footprint belongs overwhelmingly to the industrial centers of the imperialist world, the physical destruction—manifested in crop failures, severe drought, flooding, and damaged infrastructure—falls disproportionately on semicolonial societies. Framing these events as merely “natural disasters” shields the capitalist mode of production from critique and obscures climate catastrophe as an institutionalized assault on oppressed and economically vulnerable populations.

Far from resolving the agrarian question, this ecological and economic squeeze accelerates what Paris Yeros calls generalized semiproletarianization. In this condition, households that have lost all or part of their means of production do not become fully dependent on wages. Instead, they combine precarious employment with small-scale farming, petty trade, subsistence production, care work, and other sources of livelihood (Yeros, 2023). Across much of the Global South, this blurs the conventional boundary between peasant and worker and produces socially fragmented labor forces that move between rural and urban economies (Moyo & Yeros, 2005; Moyo et al., 2013; Yeros, 2024).

Under conditions of monopoly capitalism, these labor reserves can weaken workers’ bargaining power and shift the costs of social reproduction onto households and communities (Marx, 1976; Yeros, 2023). Millions may circulate between degraded smallholder farming, informal street trade, temporary migration, and precarious wage work without being absorbed into secure urban industrial employment. Rather than representing a simple transition from peasant production to wage labor, semiproletarianization describes a durable social formation in which rural and urban livelihood strategies remain interdependent (Yeros, 2023).

To propose “ecosocialism” as a generic, off-the-shelf alternative to this twin crisis, without subjecting the term itself to critical scrutiny, is to risk reproducing a dangerous conceptual trap. Much dominant Western-centered ecosocialist discourse reduces the problem to an abstract, planet-wide carbon-accounting exercise. In doing so, it can erase the national question, gloss over the unresolved agrarian question, and ignore the necessity of national-liberation struggles in …

author: karapatan
title: Contribution to the 2026 International Ecumenical Peace Convocation Seoul, Republic of Korea
content:
Contribution to the 2026 International Ecumenical Peace Convocation Seoul, Republic of Korea 09 September 2026

Cristina Palabay KARAPATAN Secretary General

Good day to everyone, and thank you for having us in the panel.

The Philippines is in a seemingly chronic state of crisis as far as human and people’s rights are concerned. The violations of human rights and international humanitarian law are systematic and systemic, which means that these are deliberate acts, which were planned methodically, instigated and funded by State authorities and actors, and that these are borne out of a system that breeds and maintains injustice, despite the Philippine government’s accession or ratification of almost all international covenants on human rights.

From the Marcos dictatorship in the 1970’s to the current Marcos the son’s administration, government campaigns pertaining to the most-often used bywords of “national security,” “peace and order,” “peace and development,” “human security,” and others have been used to justify and legitimize the gravest atrocities and the most brutal and inhumane crimes against humanity.

Filipinos are still reeling from the sham drug war of former President Rodrigo Duterte which resulted in the mass murder of more than 30,000 citizens accused of peddling or using drugs, including more than 300 children and minors who were considered “collateral damage.” The killings, conducted in the name of “peace and order,” were done during legitimate police operations or by so-called vigilante or gun-for-hire groups, but the rhetoric of Duterte made it worse – the policy made more forceful and palpable by direct statements of the former president to kill, kill, kill and his guarantees of immunity.

Under Marcos the son, the killings continue with more than a thousand people killed, according to the UP Third World Studies Center Dahas Project. Arbitrary listing of drug users or peddlers continue at the village level, and the police memoranda issued by Duterte were never rescinded, and are thus effectively enforced to this day.

Violations of human rights and international humanitarian remain unabated, Marcos the son continues the counter-insurgency programs of his predecessors.

KARAPATAN has documented 147 individuals killed by the Armed Forces of the Philippines and the Philippine National Police since July 2022, while attempted murder of 87 individuals was also recorded. Majority of the victims were poor peasants, who were publicly portrayed as armed rebels, even if their families and communities attest to the fact that they weren’t combatants.

Among those recently killed were nine civilians, including a journalist, youth organizers, and Filipino-American activists, in Negros Occidental, together with ten hors de combat. The Negros 19 as they are referred to were killed in broad daylight, in a fishpond where they had nowhere to escape to. The incident is the fourth case of massacre in the island of Negros – an island whose vast tracts of productively agricultural lands are owned by the country’s biggest landlords, while generations of peasants have tilled lands which were taken from them and when they take seasonal work, they get paid with slave wages.

Also killed were Kuni Cuba, a 16-year old student from an indigenous tribe, while he was chanced upon by soldiers when they were walking home from a community event; 16-year old Everly Kee Jacolbe who was killed with her mother and a family friend at their home in Negros Oriental; and a 4-year old boy and his 11-year old brother who were killed with their peasant activist parents in their home in Negros Occidental.

None of these killings have been thoroughly investigated by government agencies, and no perpetrator among the State forces have been made accountable.

This pattern is similar to the acts of abduction and enforced disappearances documented by KARAPATAN. Currently, there are 16 victims of enforced disappearances who remain missing to this date. This includes environmental advocates, women’s rights activists, and peace consultants. There were those who were abducted and then surfaced, and they testified that those who captured them and kept them incommunicado from their loved ones and lawyers were the soldiers. None of these enforced disappearances have been thoroughly investigated by government agencies, and no perpetrator among the State forces have been made accountable.

author: groundxero
title: The ‘Seditious’ Life of the Public University
content:
Today, as we battle to save our public universities, we must remember that what is at stake is more than just democratic practices, administrative autonomy or academic freedom.


 


Jhelum Roy


 


“I swear fidelity to the King, to his Royal successors and to the Fascist regime, and I swear to respect the [National Fascist Party’s] Statute and the other laws of the State, and to fulfil my teacher’s and all academics’ duties with the aim of preparing industrious and righteous citizens, patriotic and devoted to the Fascist regime. I swear not to be or ever become a member of organisations or parties whose activities are incompatible with my official duties.”


 


1931, Mussolini’s Italy. The state required all university professors to take a public loyalty oath in the name of the King and the fascist regime. Twelve refused, declaring the oath incompatible with their academic and political integrity. This defiance cost them their jobs, their social standing, for some even economic security. Nearly a century later, though, it is the refusal of the twelve that history memorialises in glorious details. Yet, today when we revisit this moment to make sense of our present, two questions jut out uncomfortably refusing to go away. The first asks, why did nearly 1250 academics, many of whom were not known fascists, comply? The second is perhaps even more obstinate: why did Mussolini need them to make a public display of allegiance at all? By 1931, the regime had already been taking hold of the university through quieter means: removing inconvenient academics, curtailing administrative autonomy, controlling appointments, rewarding political reliability and disciplining dissent. The hollowing out of the university had begun long before professors were asked to publicly swear.


 


So what did the oath add?


 


The oath offers part of the answer in its own language. It did not merely demand obedience. Professors were not merely being asked to refrain from opposing the regime. They were being asked to produce “industrious and righteous citizens, patriotic and devoted to the Fascist regime”. The oath publicly laid claim to the university’s purpose. It was not just a test of private conviction but rather a plebiscite imposed on the university. Despite wielding enormous power over institutions, the fascist project still needed public legitimacy and the public spectacle of assent could do what a million disciplinary notices could not. It allowed Fascism to claim not merely that it controlled the university, but that the university had chosen its place within Fascism. More importantly, the oath made clear that the battle was never only over who would teach inside the university, what could be taught and how. It was over what kind of people the university would make, what forms of association it would permit, and ultimately what future it would help reproduce.


 


So what is it in the nature and character of a public university that makes its purpose worth claiming so publicly? At its very basis, the very idea of a public university is premised on the principle that education is not a commodity but a social good that every person is entitled to. It is this very principle that makes the space of the public university answerable to certain democratic values, to practices of collective life making, and to a commitment to the society that sustains it. And, it is precisely because the university can hold open these possibilities that it has historically been such a contested site. The fact that a public university is built through collective resources, that its classrooms, libraries, laboratories, hostels, canteens, scholarships, salaries and infrastructure are sustained through the labour of the toiling masses, makes that labouring society a stakeholder in the university even if many may never step inside it. It is what makes the university ultimately answerable to this society. It is also this responsibility that bestows on the university an obligation to build democratic practices, to organise life differently and above all, to imagine that another world is possible.


 


The contestation that we see historically unfold is therefore a contestation over these possibilities of organising life, of ways of imagining society, and of reproducing democratic practices in a society that is otherwise deeply ordered through class, caste, gender, ethnic, linguistic, regional hierarchies. It is what makes libraries, classrooms, corridors …

author: Editors
title: Labor capitulates to Hanson on migration
content:
The federal government’s new “

migration plan

”, announced by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke on Thursday, is a spineless capitulation to One Nation’s constant attempts to blame migrants for Australia’s cost-of-living problems.

The primary targets in Labor’s plan are backpackers and international students. Who knew that these people, who pay thousands to be here—often for the privilege of doing crap, low-paid work—have been the problem all along.

Who isn’t the Labor Party targeting? Not the bankers squeezing billions from debt-laden workers. Not the supermarket duopoly with its fraudulent “sales” as it price fixes and gouges its way to multi-billion-dollar profits. Not the privatised aged care facilities that mint their owners untold millions every week while residents lie malnourished in their own excrement. Not the pokies venues and sports-betting companies making a killing from addicts.

Not the privatised utility companies taking a cut at every transmission point while pensioners freeze through winters and bake in summers to save power. Not the toll road operators given a license to print money off the back of commuters skipping meals so their kids can go on school excursions. Not the swarms of business owners who refuse to pay the legal minimum in wages and superannuation while their staff work two jobs.

Not the property developers and land bankers driving up housing prices. Not the bosses squeezing unpaid overtime from almost everyone in the labour force. Not the ever-expanding billionaire class that demands even lower taxes so that they can avoid contributing some of what they’ve stolen to help with hospitals and schools for their workers. Not the mining companies that help themselves by taking the country’s natural mineral endowments and selling them for private gain so Gina Rinehart can loan Pauline Hanson a private jet whenever she wants.

And certainly not the government itself, or the state governments, which refuse to build enough essential infrastructure and properly fund essential services.

No, Burke dedicated an entire National Press Club address to outline his plan to clamp down on post-adolescent Brits doing bonded labour on fruit farms (Burke will introduce a ballot for that privilege now) and students charged tens, sometimes hundreds of thousands of dollars for the privilege of listening to dull commerce lectures in which they’re told how the economy

really

 works. (Hint: it’s not the exploitation of workers leading to the concentration of wealth at the top of society; it’s market efficiency delivering housing, electricity, food and other goods and services at the

best

 prices.)

As with almost every major political issue in the 21st century—US-led wars, refugee rights, marriage equality, climate change and the environment, Indigenous rights, workers’ rights and so on—Labor politicians say nice things, responsible things ... until it looks like they might lose a few seats in parliament, or until the capitalists start campaigning against them. Then they melt like Mars bars under a hot sun.

In this case, it’s Pauline Hanson’s petty campaigning. Once again, the ALP has capitulated to avoid a fight. This characteristic is part of Labor’s DNA. Any serious fight against the right would mobilise tens of thousands in solidarity, and in a left-wing direction: against those at the top of society profiting from workers’ increasing hardships across the country. But because Labor governs for those at the top, it almost always tries to avoid upsetting them or their media mouthpieces, who invariably back the very right-wing forces that attack ALP governments.

In Labor’s quest to appease the right, to find anyone to blame—anyone except the capitalist class—it’s targeted a bunch of people that pretty much no one will leap to defend (except farmers and university administrators, on the basis that they want to keep exploiting them), so that it can seem to be doing something about the cost-of-living crisis caused by the capitalists.

This is not “smart politics” that will neutralise the rising far-right threat. This is centre-left politics accommodating the far right in real time and legitimising One Nation’s talking points.

It goes further. Ministerial Direction 110, which allows the Immigration minister to refuse or cancel visas, is to be amended to make it easier for the government to, in Burke’s words, “stamp out hatred”. Direction 110 already allows for visa cancellations based on someone’s …

author: Susan Price
title: ‘Ecological crisis creates a challenge and an opportunity for the left’
content:
Ayesha Ahmad, a Pakistani socialist-feminist activist, researcher, educator, and labour rights practitioner with the Haqooq-e-Khalq Party, was one of the guest speakers at the Ecosocialism 2026 conference in Magan-djin/Brisbane, September 11–13. She spoke to Green Left’s Peter Boyle about the impact of the mounting global ecological crisis on politics in Pakistan.

The catastrophic flash floods in Nepal as a result of global warming and the melting of the Himalayan glaciers were a warning to the world, but does it have a special significance for Pakistan, which also borders the Himalayas?

The catastrophic flash floods in Nepal are a profound warning for Pakistan. For years, Pakistan has been among the countries most exposed to the climate crisis in South Asia, and we have already witnessed what a warming Himalaya can do — from the catastrophic 2022 floods, to increasingly frequent glacial lake outburst floods in Gilgit-Baltistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The Nepal disaster tells us that we may be entering an even more dangerous phase of the Himalayan climate crisis.

But for me, there is a much deeper question here. South Asia shares a history. We share the history of colonial extraction, of loot and plunder, of resources being taken from our lands to build wealth elsewhere. Political decolonisation did not necessarily mean economic decolonisation. The geography of extraction has changed, the language has changed, but the underlying relationship can remain remarkably familiar.

Today, we are being told that the answer is development, investment, critical minerals, energy security and even the green transition. But we have to ask: whose development, whose energy security and whose transition?

Climate change cannot be reduced to mining alone. But it would be deeply irresponsible to pursue accelerated extraction in an already climate-vulnerable Himalayan region without asking what extraction does to fragile ecosystems, watersheds, communities and the cumulative resilience of the region.

And this is where the history of colonialism matters. We cannot keep repeating the old colonial bargain under a new vocabulary: our mountains provide the minerals, our communities bear the ecological and social costs and the value is extracted into global markets elsewhere.

If the Global North needs minerals for its energy transition, then the question must be: Who owns them? Who decides? Who benefits? Who bears the environmental costs? And what happens to the people and ecosystems from which these resources are extracted?

We cannot continue with an economic model that treats our mountains, minerals, rivers and land as commodities.

We cannot call it a green transition if the transition is built on another round of extraction from the Global South. We cannot decolonise our politics while continuing to colonise our resources. And we cannot keep asking the people of Pakistan to pay the climate price for a development model from which they receive so little of the wealth.

For Pakistan, the lesson from Nepal is therefore not simply to prepare better for floods.

If extraction continues without ecological limits, democratic control and justice — and if the old unequal relationship between the Global North and resource-rich countries of the Global South continues under the language of “green development” — then the next disaster will not be a surprise. It will be a consequence of choices we already made.

Many years ago, we took part in an international campaign for the release of Baba Jan from Gilgit-Baltistan, who was dubbed the “first climate justice political prisoner”. How does the mounting ecological crisis impact repression and human rights?

The struggle is not only about environmental protection, but about who has the right to speak, whose land is protected, whose losses are recognised, and whether climate-affected communities are allowed to demand justice.

For me, the story of Baba Jan is one of the clearest examples of what climate politics looks like in Pakistan when it becomes a question of justice, rather than simply a question of climate change. And this tells us something very important about the space available to the left in Pakistan.

We are allowed to talk about climate change. We are allowed to talk about floods, melting glaciers, carbon emissions and resilience. But when we start talking about climate justice — about land, ownership, displacement, workers’ rights, resource extraction, reparations and who is …

author: Anneke Demanuele
title: Albo is proud to be a houso—will anyone else get the chance?
content:
“I’m proud to be a houso, and I’m proud of the community in which I grew up.” These were the words of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, spoken with a quivering top lip, after One Nation leader Pauline Hanson attacked his mother, Maryanne Albanese, for living most of her life in a public housing unit.

“Housing commission houses should not be there for people to live in them for 30, 40 [years]”, Hanson said. “And he said his mother lived in the same one she was born in for 65 years.”

Albanese may be proud to be a houso, but his party is ensuring that very few others will be able to access the level of housing security he and his mother did. Across the country, public housing is being eroded and depleted—homes and buildings left in disrepair, demolished or sold off to private developers. The idea that the government should build and provide long-term public housing to those who need it has been almost entirely destroyed.

In Victoria, public housing has been decimated. Walk-up estates have been bulldozed to make way for luxury developments, and 44 apartment towers are scheduled for demolition. The UN special rapporteur on adequate housing, Koldo Casla, has condemned the slated demolition of the 44 towers. In his letter to the Australian government, Casla writes:

“I am concerned that affected residents have primarily been treated as occupants of public property rather than as rights-holders entitled to participate in decisions fundamentally affecting their homes and communities.”

Demolishing housing will force residents out of homes meant to be permanent, out of their communities and away from vital services and infrastructure they depend on. All in the middle of a housing crisis.

According to the Victorian Housing Peaks Alliance, Victoria needs 377,000 more social housing dwellings by 2051 to accommodate everyone who needs low-cost housing. Instead of demolishing public housing and handing over public land to private developers, the government should refurbish existing stock and build new homes.

“It must be reasonably feared that the destruction of 44 public housing towers in central locations or the city will rather amplify these problems and not be a suitable measure to address these preexisting violations of the right to adequate housing”, Casla notes.

The Victorian Labor government says that the total number of dwellings will increase. But it will cut public housing unit numbers significantly. They will be replaced by a mix of community housing, run by not-for-profit agencies, and private dwellings sold at market rates. Tenants have fewer rights, face higher costs, enjoy less long-term housing security and are more easily evicted from community housing as compared to public housing. Data from the Australian Institute of Housing and Welfare in 2023, for instance, shows that when comparing public and community housing tenure length, the proportion of public housing residents that have lived in their homes for more than a decade is twice that of the community housing sector.

Residents in inner-city suburbs will and have been shunted off to outer suburbs, far from the schools, kindergartens and other services they rely on and that connect them with others. Many won’t be able to return to public housing at all.

This adds to the general erosion of the idea that housing is a human right that should be guaranteed to all. Instead of being an option for working-class people to live in, raise their families and build their communities over a lifetime, public housing is increasingly seen as a temporary option for only the most desperate—those living in extreme poverty and for whatever reason unable to participate in the labour market. Today, it is being deliberately run down to make its demolition or sell-off inevitable.

Public housing in Australia has always fallen below the standard of Britain and Western Europe. Writing in the

Marxist Left Review

, Jordan Humphreys details the limitations: “Access to public housing would be restricted to those on very low incomes, so it would be put aside only for the very poorest of the poor. If not enough of the poor could be found, then the Housing Commissions were encouraged to sell off ‘excess’ housing stock”. By the 1960s, two-thirds of British people lived in public housing, compared to only 4.2 percent of Australians (today it is about 2.6 percent).

The Victorian government’s housing strategy document describes public housing as a “legacy”, and what remains is intended …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Socialist Alliance trade unionists to contest Western Victoria Region
content:
Socialist Alliance in Victoria has announced candidates for the Legislative Council in the Western Victoria Region at the November 28 elections.

The party is running on the campaign theme of “Fighting for people, not the billionaires”.

Tim Gooden, Sue Bull and Ross Smith are active trade unionists from the construction and maritime industries, and think progressive working class people need to be heard.

Gooden, a former Secretary of Geelong Trades Hall and a Palestine justice campaigner, told Green Left: “We are putting forward positive solutions for workers rather than the hate which is being put out by the big end of town. Blaming migrants and refugees for cost-of-living rises is about scapegoating people who have nothing. Meanwhile, the billionaires rake in profits.”

Bull, a teacher trainer in schools and the construction industry for many years told GL: “State and federal governments can always find money to subsidise their big business mates, but when it comes to funding housing, health or education, the coffers are bare. We need to build a movement that fights for us and our needs.”

Smith, a maritime industry union stalwart, said the ongoing industry closures in the region has led to hidden poverty and intense anger. “Lots of money is going towards the war machine. Why can’t we have good long-term jobs in renewable industries or manufacturing industries that create rather than destroy?”

Socialist Alliance in Geelong is also running candidates in all the electorates in the district.

[Get in touch with Victorian Socialist Alliance to help out and donate to the campaign.]

author: AWSM
title: The anarchist case for abstentionism in elections
content:
The right to vote is seen by most as a necessary prerequisite for freedom across the world. People have fought and died for the right to vote in elections. Women across the world fought bitter battles for the right to vote. So why should anarchists question this as a right worth having?

The entire electoral show is designed to encourage us to believe that not only does our vote matter, but that it is the most important decision we could possibly make. Indeed, voting is held so sacred by many that the mere mention of not voting is enough to cause outrage. Pointing out that our vote makes no difference anyway, will see you accused of being apathetic, privileged, immature, and even being part of the alt-right!

But as noted anarchist Vernon Richards wrote,

“So long as we have capitalism and government, the job of anarchists is to fight both, and at the same time encourage people to take what steps they can to run their own lives.” [“Anarchists and Voting,” pp. 176–87, The Raven, No. 14, p. 179].

Electoralism ensures that a statist perspective becomes dominant. Everything is seen in terms of state intervention and following the decisions of the leaders, which has always proved deadly to encouraging a spirit of revolt, self-management, and self-help – the very keys to creating change in a society. Rather than being something other people discuss on behalf of working-class people, anarchists argue that politics should not be a specialised activity in the hands of the so-called experts (i.e., politicians) but instead lie in the hands of those directly affected by it in the process of participation, direct action, and self-management. Those that channel any “political” conclusions into electoral politics distort discussions into only what is possible within the current system. Given this, is it surprising that anarchists argue that the people “must organise their powers apart from and against the State?” [Bakunin, The Political Philosophy of Bakunin, p. 376].

Abstentionists get told, “If you don’t vote, you have no right to complain about the outcome,” but we consider the opposite to be true. It is those who have voted, who have agreed to the rules, and agreed to be governed by the winners who cannot complain. It is those who do not participate who have the right to complain about the outcome more than anyone else.

We get told that the reality is that voting does change things, but we can, and do, deny that. Voting attempts to provide the population with the illusion of change while in reality it reinforces the current system. A policy here and there may change, the faces may change, but the system of a wealthy minority ruling a poorer majority remains. People will continually be telling us that abstaining from voting will help the right-wing win the election, that it is better if the lesser evil wins. This may possibly be the case (although the argument is far from convincing), but why should we base our society on a compromise with evil? In fact, the “progressive” left wing party you vote for will often be ready to take the same actions as a right-wing government when it comes to imposing anti-working-class action upon us, (as we shall show later in this essay the state has a corrupting effect on those who enter politics with high principles). There should be a better way, and we say the dismantling of government, in all its existing and potential forms is that way.

Most of the left wing in Aotearoa, and quite a few people who claim to identify as anarchists, will support reformist parties in the upcoming election. You will hear them saying things like “vote Labour (or Green) without illusions,” or “vote Labour/Green but build a socialist alternative.” The slogans that these others may shout only reflect the idea that change can and should be brought about by a small number of elite politicians. Abstentionists do not say things like this. There are many problems with our electoral system of democracy, which we shall run through, but we must state that first and foremost, as anarchists, we see voting as against running contrary to our anti-statist and anti-hierarchy principles, and we see electoralism as contrary to our goals and practice. It reinforces the idea that society is divided into order-givers and order-takers. Famed French anarchist, Elisee Reclus, put it well when he said,

“Everything that can be said about the suffrage may be summed up in a sentence. To vote is to give up your own power. To elect a …

author: Nick Reich
title: Largest strike of road transport workers in decades demands better pay and conditions
content:
The chants of several hundred striking truck drivers boomed from the steps of Victorian Trades Hall on the morning of 10 September: “When we fight, we win!”

The fight involves several workplaces around the country that united for a 24-hour strike. In Victoria, workers at FedEx, Border Express, K&S Chemtrans, Sadleirs and Qube all voted to take simultaneous action. Nationally, more than 5,000 workers walked off the job. The Transport Workers Union (TWU) officials claim that this strike is the largest road transport strike in Australian history.

Despite working for different companies, the issues striking truckers face are almost identical. Low wages, lack of job security and increasing pressures to do unsafe work. Across the industry, new companies increasingly undercut established, unionised companies by underpaying drivers and forcing them into higher-volume, unsafe work patterns. Road transport is no less essential than it was 30 years ago for the delivery of our food, fuel, medical supplies and other essentials, but over that time, the people driving the trucks have seen their wages go backwards and their working conditions become increasingly unsafe.

Colin, a driver for K&S Chemtrans, told me at the strike rally that over the twenty years he has been driving, “the industry has become much more competitive. We used to rank number one in dangerous goods delivery, but now we’re total rubbish”. K&S has gone through multiple sales and restructures during Colin’s time there. “We don’t cart milk and honey, you know. What we move is dangerous, toxic, and sometimes carcinogenic. And still our dangerous goods allowance is below the award!”

Workers started the bargaining process with K&S last July, asking for a substantial above-inflation pay rise, among other things. After a year of slow-moving negotiations, the company offered a 15.5 percent pay rise over three years, with no back pay for the year of negotiation. Workers were rightly insulted by this offer, since it would only barely edge above inflation and do nothing to close the gap of almost $15 an hour between K&S drivers and those doing the same work at Toll. Due to the resulting anger, union membership at Colin’s site in Truganina has climbed to around 97 percent.

At FedEx, it is a similar story. Negotiations there have been dragging on for months, with the company offering the workers an insulting pay rise of less than 11 percent over three years. As previously

reported

, the use of direct service contracts on piece rates to undermine employed drivers is a big issue. I asked one driver about what, if any, tactics the FedEx bosses had used to pressure workers into accepting their offer; he responded:

“What haven’t they done! They’ve illegally disadvantaged workers by cancelling their weekend work; they’ve responded to our 24-hour strike by locking us out for another 24 hours; they’ve even talked about shutting-up shop in Australia and leaving us all out of a job. Plus, they had yard meetings and toolbox meetings almost every day last week to try and pressure workers into voting up their shit agreement.”

Even with these bullying tactics, FedEx workers voted down the same agreement twice, although by a slimmer margin on the second vote. One driver explained the union culture: “Us old drivers, the ones who were around when the company was still TNT, we’re the core of the union. It’s in our blood. For us, once you go union, you’re union for life”. It is a staunch sentiment, but it also implies a concern about younger drivers joining the company who aren’t yet “union for life” and are more likely to accept worse conditions.

Another FedEx driver, who had been in the union for 40 years, chimed in: “When I first started, everyone was union. And we’d strike for our rights all the time. We’d have a 24-hour strike if there wasn’t enough sugar for our tea!” That sort of unionism is what the bosses of FedEx, and every other transport company, want to extinguish. He went on, “We had to fight for our conditions, and now the young folk are going to have to step up and draw a line before they take it all away”.

While the 10 September strike was the largest in some decades, it involved only a relatively small section of the union’s membership. It did not include the union’s best organised workforces in big companies like Linfox, Toll and Team Global Express, for example. Most of them recently signed deals locking in wage rises just below the current rate of inflation for …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Ecosocialism 2026 forges unity and builds struggles
content:
“The big people behind capitalism are quite aware that they are planning the end of the world as we know it”, Sabrina Fernandes, a political economist and ecosocialist activist from Brazil, told the Ecosocialism 2026 conference in Magan-djin/Brisbane, September 11–13.

“They don’t have a problem with the world ending as we know it — as long as they can keep making profits,” Fernandes said.

“They do have a problem with a society that they might not be able to control when things get really hard, as we are coming to this stage of ecocide and global catastrophe. They are fighting over the spoils of war and climate change.”

Places that would not normally be considered part of the grab are becoming so, Fernandes said. The oceans “are a new terra nullius for them” — for ocean floor mining.

There should be an international agreement for this, but US President Donald Trump does not care and has begun issuing his own licences, she added.

Helen Yaffe, author, activist and Professor of Latin American Political Economy, University of Glasgow, told the conference that socialist Cuba, one of the key targets of Trump’s new colonialism, is facing multiple and mounting challenges as the US blockade intensifies.

The response that she has witnessed, in a recent visit to Cuba, was: “We shall not submit!”

“Revolutionary Cuba wrote the rulebook on resilience,” Yaffe said. Facing a total oil blockade since January, Cuba is now undertaking an incredibly rapid transition to renewable energies.

“Many commentators are saying this will be the fastest ever transition.” Solar panel parks now supply more than 60% of electricity on some days, but Yaffe said the challenge is storage.

Singaporean ecosocialist See Yong Feng, another guest speaker, told Green Left that capitalism is holding back human development.

“The need for limitless economic growth is often framed as the only way to solve global poverty, but new research strongly disproves this. The world already uses way more than enough energy and materials to provide a decent standard of living for all, but the profit-driven capitalist system prevents this from happening.

“We can both address poverty and the climate crisis, as long as we break the capitalist elites’ control of our economy and democratise our production and consumption,” See said.

The Gaza genocide, Trump’s blatant disregard for international and domestic laws and his naked colonial violence symbolise the ugly reality that is forging a new generation of activists, Alex Bainbridge, a conference organiser, told GL.

“Trump has his admirers and imitators all around the world, including Marine Le Pen in France, Narendra Modi in India and Pauline Hanson here.

“But while far-right politicians push hard, there is a sharp reaction and a growing resistance; this conference was a powerful reminder of that,” Bainbridge said.

Remah Naji, a leading activist with Justice for Palestine Magan-djin, expressed this resistance. “Maybe we can’t stop a fascist and psychopath like Netanyahu from committing the war crimes he’s committing … but I can hold my government to account.”

The conference included a solidarity concert with Phil Monsour and an art exhibition.

Markela Panegyres, another conference organiser and curator of the art exhibition, told GL: “From the ongoing genocide in Gaza, to the endless drive to more wars and militarism, to ecocide, to the rise of the far right, the depravity of US-led imperialism and global capitalism is reaching ever-higher levels.

“The gravity of this moment demands that art and artists play an active role in resistance.

“This is why the concept of cultural intifada is so important: Art should not be merely a reflection of life, or entertainment or a commodity, but a weapon in the struggle for our collective liberation.

“The work of the artists, musicians and theatre makers who participated in the cultural intifada round-table and exhibition demonstrated the importance of art in movement-building.

“We were so proud that Aunty Sue Coleman-Haseldine, a senior Googatha Elder, Maralinga survivor and long-term anti-nuclear activist, came all the way from the Googatha Nation in the west of South Australia, north of Ceduna.”

Coleman-Haseldine talked about the campaign against rocket and weapons testing on her Country and her opposition to AUKUS and to US military and surveillance bases.

Ecosocialism 2026 was sponsored by the Socialist Alliance, Green Left, Resistance Books and Links — International …

title: “There’s this sketchy Dutch black metal band touring Australia …”
content:
I was contacted a little while ago by somebody raising concerns about a couple of upcoming black metal gigs. Below is the text they sent.

There’s this sketchy Dutch black metal band, Helleruin, playing in Melbourne at the Northcote Social Club on September 11 and in Sydney at Crowbar on September 12.

Most of Helleruin’s records have been released on New Era Productions, which has put out a number of releases by fash black metal bands and which is run by Jasper Velzel, a NSBM and RAC musician. In addition, another project of Helleruin’s Carchost — Orewoet — is on the label Heidens Hart, which — along with releasing some far-right stuff — is owned by a former live guitarist of prominent fash band Graveland.

Moreover, a number of the local supporting acts have sketchy connections.

Order of Orias, one of two supports in Melbourne along with Petrol (see below), are on World Terror Committee, which releases fashy stuff and is owned by Sven Zimper, a member of prominent NSBM group Absurd.

Of the bands playing Sydney with Helleruin (Krvna, Pestilential Shadows, Destruktor, Vicissitude, Gravgöt, Grotesque Bliss, Petrol, Blasfemancia and Akhoth) at the ‘Call from the Grave’ festival:

Pestilential Shadows have released music on the Chinese label, GoatowaRex, who are very friendly to NSBM acts. Additionally, PS is part of a collective called Ordo Ater Anguis/Order of the Black Serpent, which includes numerous far right acts. Michael W Ford of Black Funeral appears to be a former Order of Nine Angles (09A) member in the United States who — after distancing himself from O9A — attempted to formulate a social Darwinist version of the Satanic Temple (lol), which coalesce around the Australian fash-friendly label, Dark Adversary. Indeed, one of the members of PS is also a member of Varw, a band on Dark Adversary. Further, Akhoth released a demo, ‘Storm of Pagan Fury’, on CD on Dark Adversary this year.

Grotesque Bliss are on Iron Bonehead which, along with the suspect name, appears to be run by a (if only barely) crypto-fascist.

Destruktor is on a label, Hells Headbangers, which has previously released and re-released stuff by Satanic Warmaster and Deströyer 666, including re-releasing Deströyer 666’s debut album, ‘Unchain the Wolves’, on a few different mediums over the last few years. Additionally, Inquisition had a few releases on Hells Headbangers after their lead singer (who is also a Satanist pedo) released openly fash music on fash label Satanic Skinhead Propaganda (a label which the Iron Bonehead guy sold in his old fash-friendly record store).

The most recent (2024) EP of Krvna, formally of PS, was released on Zazen Sounds, run by Greek nazi black metaller Acherontass of Αχέροντας (Krvna played guest guitar on their most recent album). For what it’s also worth, Third Eye Temple — the Polish label on which Krvna’s 2022 album was released — have released one split and re-issued an EP by Voidhanger, a side project of Polish far right black metallers, Infernal War.

Finally, Petrol were previously on a cancelled bill with Gurn. They also played a gig with Japanese band Abigail, who are signed to Nuclear Now Productions, a fash-friendly label linked to Iron Bonehead (similarly exposed by the nsbmboneheads blog linked above). In addition, Petrol played at Crowbar Sydney last year with Bolzer (see nsbmboneheads blog), who released all but their last record on Iron Bonehead. The other headliner was Portal, who have released lots of records on Hells Headbangers including, recently, a split with Blood of Kingu — a side-project of the Ukrainian ultra-nationalists from Drudkh — on the label in 2014.

author: Deaglan Godwin
title: Another property developer collapses. We need to abolish them entirely
content:
The collapse of Bathla Group, a multi-billion-dollar property developer, illustrates how broken housing is in Australia.

Bathla entered voluntary administration in late August after it could no longer repay almost $3.4 billion in debt. Its collapse has left hundreds of workers unpaid and unemployed, and hundreds of buyers in limbo. The company owes millions to subcontractors and suppliers.

Bathla made immense profits from building dodgy houses and apartments in western Sydney. Harris Mazoudier, who purchased an apartment from Bathla in Schofields, spoke to the

Sydney Morning Herald

 about the defects that littered his unit. Like many other property developers, Bathla has struggled to admit responsibility for these problems.

Profits also came from unsafe work practices. In 2015, a surveyor on a Bathla site fell nearly four metres and was impaled on concrete bars. SafeWork fined the company just $135,000 despite the surveyor’s long-term injuries. Industrial accidents are never treated with the same severity as criminal cases of the same magnitude.

Bathla’s founder, Bhart Bhushan, was once nicknamed “the Baron of Blacktown”. This appropriately sums up the power that property developers have over housing and urban planning. They wield this power to ensure the highest short-term profits, regardless of the social, economic and environmental consequences.

Baron Bhushan had a track record of using lawsuits to bully councils into approving his development applications. According to former Blacktown Mayor Stephen Bali, the council racked up $1 million a year in legal fees after slightly reducing the number of units in Bathla’s development proposals.

Before you weep for the baron’s downfall, know that construction continues on the family’s $5.5 million Dural mansion. “Sierra Morena”, named after a Spanish mountain range, features several swimming pools, a four-car detached garage and a basketball court. Renovation work is still underway to expand this palatial dwelling to include another garage and a “French fan cobblestone” driveway, whatever that is. Somehow, business owners have an uncanny way of never letting a corporate collapse get in the way of their own luxury lifestyle.

The ideologues of the system tell us that the free market is the most efficient way to allocate resources in our society. The profit-seeking of individual enterprises allegedly results in the best outcomes for consumers and society more broadly. Housing in Australia shows the exact opposite.

Defective apartments and injured workers are inevitable consequences of developers and construction companies seeking to cut costs and maximise profits. The pressure to build the houses as quickly as possible with as little delay, in order to cash in on Sydney’s inflated housing market, produces example after example of this. A 2021 survey found that four in ten new apartment buildings have serious defects. According to SafeWork, 44 construction workers died in Australia in 2024.

The anarchic housing market system does not ensure the best outcome for renters, homebuyers or society as a whole. The private housing market has delivered immense profits to developers, banks and landlords. But it has given most workers rental stress and burdensome mortgages: average unit rents have increased 65 percent in the last six years; average house prices have grown by 60 percent.

Property developers have reshaped how our city looks and works—for the worse. Developers build with an eye only to profit, not to holistic urban planning. The amenities people need—schools, parks, public transport, community spaces—are never their concern. Bathla currently owes an unspecified amount to Blacktown City Council for public infrastructure improvements it had committed to building. The worst-hit spots of Sydney are precisely those in the west, where existing urban infrastructure is not designed for increasingly dense populations.

The housing market is propped up by government policies, contrary to claims from free-market apologists. Tax policies such as negative gearing and capital gains tax discount incentivise investment and speculation. The hue and cry from the establishment about the Albanese government’s minor tax changes shows how well the property market has operated as a wealth generator for a minority. The policies remain government interference in the market—interference in favour of the rich.

Every scheme announced by the government to build more homes simply puts …
