author: David Swanson
title: Abolish the Board of Peace. Try the Table of Peace.
content:
Nonviolent Activism, North America, What to do

By David Swanson, World BEYOND War, September 5, 2026

I don’t mean to complain about the Board of Peace. If you want to ensure endless wars, expand settler colonialism, formally empower oligarchs over nations, destroy the United Nations, and keep genocides rolling along, I’m sure it’s fantastic!

But I recommend, at least in addition, trying the table of peace. This is something I tried in Charlottesville, Virginia, on Saturday. First, you’ll need a table. Then you’ll need some supplies. I recommend free stickers, bookmarks, and flyers, some books, some sign up sheets, some display boards, a jar for donations, a banner. Bring all this stuff and a few friendly people to a farmer’s market.

And you’ll need one more thing: a game. Here’s how I did that. I asked people to pretend to be the United States Congress for 10 seconds. (Many of them were disgusted at the thought but I assured them they could shower afterwards.) Then I gave them 12 stones and told them it was the federal discretionary budget for 2027. I asked them to distribute the stones in eight glasses labeled: Environmental Protection; Education; Labor, Small Business Administration, and Commerce; Health and Human Services; Housing and Urban Development, Interior, and Transportation; War and war preparations; Energy; and Other. If they asked “Now is this green energy or fossil fuel energy?” or “Is this education as it should be done or the dy$#@! they do now?” then I told them it was their ideal form of energy or education.

A lot of people played the game.

Environmental Protection won. Very close behind that were Education and Health and Human Services. Not far behind those was Energy, which everyone told me was renewable energy. Housing and Labor came next. And one gentleman the entire time I was tabling put one stone into War. He explained, almost apologetically, that it was for the “defensive wars.” I backed away slowly and kept my eyes on him.

When each person had finished distributing the stones, I showed them a pie chart illustrating the budget proposed for 2027 by Trump. The glass that people had left almost empty eats up 77.66% of the pie. The categories people wanted funded most get the tiniest slivers.

Not everybody will play the game. Some people will take a sticker and keep walking without slowing down. Some people will stop and talk. Others will buy a book, sign a pledge, etc. With the ones who will devote 60 seconds or more, your goal is of course to get them engaged. Will they sign up and get involved? Will they take some flyers to distribute? Here, I think, it’s important to understand that success is measured in very small numbers. If you can get a few people doing more than they were before, that’s a win.

Many people, those who don’t slow down and those who stop to chat, will assure you that all is fine because they plan to vote in an election. I live in a district and state and nation with no anti-war candidates running for any offices, but even if that were not the case, the delusion that voting fixes everything and that no one can do anything other than voting would still be by far the single biggest hurdle to effective participation in society.

Many will tell you how deeply they agree regarding war and peace, and how sorry they are that all is hopeless and doomed by “human nature,” or “sociopaths,” or “money” — they’ve got a million of these. Others will thank you for what you’re doing — conveying the meaning that they’re glad you’re doing it so that they don’t have to.

But there’s usually a few percent who will actually get active and educate and agitate and demonstrate. Get them, and you’ll have done your part toward finding that few percent of the whole population that is needed to change the world.

content:
Le groupe local de Paris de l'

UCL

 vous invite à la projection du film

Agent Orange, une bombe à retardement

.


Le groupe local Paris Nord Est de l'Union Communiste Libertaire vous invite à une projection-débat autour du film

Agent Orange, une bombe à retardement

, de Thuy Tien Ho et Laurent Lindebrings.


En quittant le Vietnam en 1975, l'armée américaine a laissé un poison invisible : la dioxine. Cette arme chimique puissante, plus connue sous le nom d'Agent Orange, produite par la multinationale Monsanto, a pris possession de la terre, des eaux, de la végétation. En s'infiltrant dans les sols, les rivières, elle touche la chaine alimentaire. Des millions de Vietnamiens sont victimes de la dioxine, atteints de malformations et de cancers. 40 ans après les derniers épandages, la dioxine continue ses ravages. C'est cette utilisation massive de produit toxique qui a conduit à théoriser la notion d'écocide.


Alors qu'une manifestation se prépare le 3 octobre pour protester contre les pesticides, cette projection et la discussion qui suivra seront l'occasion de se rappeler de l'utilisation des pesticides comme arme de guerre, de soulever l'importance de lutter contre le colonialisme chimique et pour une écologie anti-impérialiste.


Rendez-vous à le Jeudi 17 Septembre à 19h30 à l'

EDMP

, 8 impasse Crozatier, Paris 12

e

author: Unknown
title: İbtisam Azem: Filistinliler için hatırlamak, silinen tarihle bağı korumanın bir yolu
content:
Bir sabah bütün Filistinlilerin yok olduğu bir dünyaya uyansak ne olurdu? Filistinli yazar İbtisam Azem’in Türkçe çevirisi yakın zamanda yayımlanan romanı 

Kayboluş Kitabı

 bu soruyu ele alıyor ve kayboluşun ardından yaşananları Yafalı Alâ ile İsrailli komşusu Ariel üzerinden anlatıyor.


Tayyibe doğumlu olan ve bugün New York’ta Birleşmiş Milletler muhabirliği yapan Azem, romanını 2014 yılında anadili Arapça olarak yayımladı.

Kayboluş Kitabı

, daha sonra birçok dile çevrildi. O yıllarda yalnızca bir romanın kurgusu olan bu soru, Gazze’de üç yıla yaklaşan soykırımla birlikte bugün başka türlü okunuyor. Azem ise romandaki kayboluşu hiçbir zaman distopik bir fantezi olarak görmediğini söylüyor. Ona göre bu kayboluş, 1948’de yüz binlerce Filistinlinin sürülmesinin ve o günden beri kesintisiz süren “sessiz Nakba”nın bir yankısı.


Biz de kitaptan yola çıkarak Azem’le ‘48 Filistinlilerinin devletin okulda öğrettiği tarihle evde duyduğu tarih arasında büyümesini, hatırlamanın neden bir direniş biçimi olduğunu, 1967 işgalini eleştiren ama 1948’i sorgulamayan Ariel karakteri üzerinden İsrail’deki “makul” çoğunluğun suç ortaklığını ve Filistin edebiyatının ancak felaket anlarında ilgi görmesini konuştuk.


*İbtisam Azem, Kayboluş Kitabı (Arapçadan çeviren: Zafer Ceylan), Yapı Kredi Yayınları, 192 sayfa, 2026. 


“Nakba, hafızanın aktarımını kesintiye uğrattı”


Alâ defterine “Sanki son can simidim hafızaymış gibi…” yazıyor ama bir yandan da “Keşke daha çok sorsaydım ona” pişmanlığını dile getiriyor.

Kayboluş Kitabı

, hatırlamaya çoğu zaman geç kalmanın ve sorulamamış soruların da anlatısı. İsrail’in yok saymaya çalıştığı ‘48 Filistinlileri ve halkın kesintisiz süren varoluş mücadelesi düşünüldüğünde; “hatırlamak” Filistinliler için ne anlama geliyor ve bu “geç kalmışlık” duygusu sizde nasıl bir yer tutuyor?


Filistinliler için hatırlamak yalnızca geriye bakma edimi değil. Kim olduğumuzla, mekânlarımızla ve çoğu zaman bilinçli biçimde kenara itilmiş ya da silinmiş bir tarihle bağımızı korumanın bir yolu. Hâkim anlatı size tarihinizin ya hiç yaşanmadığını ya da yalnızca geçmişe ait olduğunu söylemeye çalıştığında, hafıza bir direniş biçimine dönüşebiliyor.


Bu, ‘48 Filistinlileri için özellikle önemli, çünkü çoğumuz resmî olarak öğretilen tarihle (devletin okulda anlattığı tarihle) evde duyduğumuz tarih arasındaki boşlukta büyüdük.


Romanda Alâ, anneannesine daha çok soru sormamış olmaktan pişmanlık duyuyor. Bu çok insani bir duygu bence. Anne babamıza ve büyüklerimize hayatlarını, çocukluklarını, evlerini, tanıdıkları insanları sormak için hep daha çok vaktimiz olacağını varsayarız. Sonra bir anda o vakit biter. Biri ölür ve asla dinleyemeyeceğiniz hikâyeler, asla soramayacağınız sorular olduğunu fark edersiniz.


Nakba insanları yalnızca fiziksel olarak yerinden etmedi, aynı zamanda hafızanın aktarımını kesintiye uğrattı ve o hafızanın içinde yaşadığı toplulukları yok etti.


Sözlü tarihin romanda bu kadar önemli olmasının sebebi bu. Yazı kaybedilen her şeyi geri getiremez, hafızadaki her boşluğu dolduramaz. Ama parçaları koruyabilir ve onları taşıyan kişinin ötesine geçmelerini sağlayabilir. Anneannenin hikâyeleri Alâ’nın hafızasının parçası oluyor, sonra Alâ’nın yazdıkları o hikâyelerin bir başkasına ulaşmasını sağlıyor.


Hatırlamak geçmişe hapsolmak anlamına gelmiyor. Tam tersine, farklı bir gelecek istediğimiz için hatırladığımızı düşünüyorum. Sömürgeleştirilenlere sık sık geçmişe saplandıkları ve artık ilerlemeleri gerektiği söylenir, oysa bugüne nasıl geldiğinizi anlamayı reddederseniz farklı bir gelecek kuramazsınız. Hatırlamak bir bakıma geçmişin yeniden gelecek olmasını engelleme çabası.


“Yafa benim bir parçam oldu”

author: Susan Price
title: Singapore’s unfinished anti-colonial struggle
content:
The dominant history of modern Singapore was meticulously constructed under the banner of the “Singapore Story”. By presenting the material interests of the ruling elite as the universal interests of the nation, the state narrative reduces the mass anti-imperialist movement of the mid-20th century into a fable; one wherein a heroic bourgeois leadership single-handedly navigates a vulnerable island state through the perils of communism to construct a prosperous capitalist metropolis.

In his six-part oral history series with Pintjin (PJ) Thum, Dr Poh Soo Kai, former student activist, co-founder of the People’s Action Party (PAP) and the Barisan Sosialis (Socialist Front) — and former political prisoner detained for nearly 17 years without trial — delivers a vital historical materialist counter-narrative.

In 36 minutes of personal testimony, Poh unpacks the class dynamics, state coercion, and geopolitical shake-ups that dismantled working-class power and shaped Singapore's transition into a disciplined capitalist state.

Poh begins by recalling how post-World War II Malayan households were adorned with portraits of Indonesia’s Sukarno, India’s Nehru and Gandhi, and China’s Chiang Kai-Shek, who were seen as regional anti-colonial leaders. The struggle in Singapore was bound to broader anti-imperialist movements across Malaya, Indonesia, and Vietnam.

Poh’s account of the 1954 Fajar Trial undermines the state’s origin myth, which positions the trial of eight members of the editorial board of Fajar (Dawn) — the University of Malaya Socialist Club’s newspaper — as Lee Kuan Yew’s (LKY’s) personal legal breakthrough.

[Editor’s note: Harry Lee Kwan Yew co-founded the PAP, was a barrister and opposition figure and became Singapore’s first Prime Minister in 1959.]

As president of the University of Malaya Socialist Club, Poh helped publish Fajar, an anti-colonial paper opposing the anti-communist South East Asian Treaty Organisation (SEATO) and foreign military bases. When the editorial board was charged with sedition, Queen’s Counsel DN Pritt arrived to lead the defense. Poh recounts Pritt greeting him warmly at the Dolphin Hotel before turning to LKY, who was acting as local junior counsel, and saying, “Harry, now you can go.”

Pritt dismissed LKY specifically to formulate an anti-colonial strategy directly with the student activists, recognising that the trial was a political battlefield rather than a legal technicality.

This moment symbolises the clash between the radical student movement and LKY’s legalism, and how official history later repackaged a left-wing victory as an LKY solo masterstroke.

As the PAP rose to power, internal contradictions between its left-wing mass base and moderate leadership erupted.

Poh recounts how the left wing consistently pushed for true self-determination, confronting PAP Chair Toh Chin Chye to issue a public statement supporting then-Chief Minister David Marshall’s 1956 call for internal self-rule — a move that infuriated LKY upon his return from London.

[Editor’s note: Marshall was appointed Chief Minister after contesting the 1955 election as a candidate for the Labour Front. After failing to secure self-rule, he resigned as Chief Minister in June 1956.]

Chief Minister Lim Yew Hock’s violent crackdowns on trade unions and Chinese school students from 1956 onward served a dual purpose: suppressing working-class organisation while allowing LKY to position himself as the sensible alternative acceptable to British imperial interests and local capital.

When dissident MPs and activists walked out to form the Barisan Sosialis in 1961, every PAP branch including LKY’s own Tanjong Pagar constituency defected to the new party. The PAP was left as a hollow electoral vessel without organic mass support.

To preempt an electoral defeat, the state deployed Operation Coldstore in February 1963. Officially framed as a security operation against a communist plot tied to the 1962 Brunei Revolt, Coldstore was a draconian political purge that sought to decapitate the political opposition, dismantle union leadership and ensure PAP hegemony.

The state weaponised identity politics to divide the multi-ethnic working-class by branding Chinese-educated labour leaders and Barisan Sosialis members as “Chinese chauvinists”. It replaced class-based solidarity with state-directed multiracialism that contained labour organising within non-threatening boundaries.

title: History Keeps Happening - Anarchists and Fellow Travellers on Palestine
content:
Author

: History Keeps Happening

Title

: Anarchists and Fellow Travellers on Palestine

Date

: September 2026

Notes

: An intro to a collection of articles.

Source

: Retrieved on September 3, 2026 from

historykeepshappening.wordpress.com


 Historically speaking, anarchists have never had a unified stance on Palestine or Zionism. Even anarchists who shared an opposition to Zionism didn’t necessarily oppose it for the same reasons, nor did they necessarily have any concern whatsoever for Palestinians.


 On the one hand, there were historical Jewish anarchists such as Emma Goldman and Joseph Cohen, who claimed to be against Zionism but at the same time dismissed or ignored the role of British imperialism and Zionist colonialism in the oppression of Palestinians.


 Goldman and Cohen rejected Zionism due to their abstract anti-nationalism. They were concerned solely with the detrimental effect of the Jewish nationalist movement on the Jewish people and the broader international working class, minus any particular regard for Palestinians as Palestinians.


 Goldman, in 1906 had already published a comrade’s anti-Zionist article in her periodical, Mother Earth. However, in 1938 she wrote her own article defending the Zionist colonization of Palestine, ignoring the repression of Palestinians by the British, and deploying Zionist mythology and John Locke’s theory of property to justify Zionist land theft. Goldman claimed, in a standard colonial trope, that Jewish settlers had gained rights to Palestinian territory because they had “tilled the soil... reclaimed wastelands and... turned them into fertile fields and blooming gardens.”


 Reginald Reynolds, a gentile fellow traveller of anarchists, responded to Goldman most appropriately at the time, criticizing her Lockean/Zionist argument, pointing out that by her “till the soil” logic, “the land in Palestine should have belonged to the Arab peasant,” and that “‘finding is keeping’ is a good motto for conquistadores and imperialists, but not, I should have thought, for Anarchists.”


 Joseph Cohen, in his 1945 book on the Jewish anarchist movement in America, callously dismissed out of hand the idea that Palestinians might have been resisting British and Zionist imperialism during the disturbances of 1929.

(The Jewish Anarchist Movement in America, 2024 English edition, pg.540)


 On the other hand, there were historical Jewish anarchists such as Marcus Graham and Albert Meltzer who did just the opposite of Goldman and Cohen, specifically highlighting British imperialism and Zionist colonialism as crucial factors for anarchists to tackle.


 This split also applied to historical gentile anarchists. On the one side there was Camillo Berneri and Vernon Richards, calling out British imperialism and Zionist colonialism, and on the other, George Woodcock, reiterating the Zionist/Lockean myth that settlers made the desert bloom and naively describing the kibbutz movement as holding shared principles with anarchists.

(Freedom: Anarchist Fortnightly, Oct.18, 1947)


 In 1986, the Jewish American anarchists Murray Bookchin and Sam Dolgoff wrote an article and a book chapter, respectively, defending the State of Israel.


 Bookchin, in his article, tossed aside any concern for Western imperialism and even spuriously claimed that the problem was just war in the abstract, that the “partition lines that were eventually established after the 1948 invasions were the product of bloody warfare — literally the give-and-take of battle — not of ‘imperialistic’ or ‘land-grabbing Zionists.’”


 Dolgoff, in his book chapter, went so far as to support the claim made by his Israeli comrades that against the Arab states, “Israel must be defended.”


 Anarchist incoherence around Palestine and Zionism should come as no surprise, however, given that European and Euro-American anarchists don’t exactly have a perfect track record when it comes to Indigenous peoples in general, nor have they been consistent in rejecting collaboration with the State (see Spain in the 1930s or Ukraine today.)


 Furthermore, abstract anarchist universalism, however well-intentioned it may be, is no ready-made and automatic solution to particularity, and Palestine perhaps has shown this more clearly than anywhere else. An attention to the specifics of settler colonialism, its imperialist backing, and the dynamics of Palestinian history is necessary, now more than ever.


 As the infamous Russian anarchist Mikhail …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Big data and the AUKUS war machine
content:
The world’s greatest remilitarisation since the World War II is underway, driven by the imperatives of the flailing United States empire.

The AUKUS war pact places us at the centre of this drive towards war. How should we imagine Australia’s role in the world?

Australia is not just a settler-colonial state; it is a sub-imperial power that has transferred subordination from its one-time colonial ruler, Britain, to the US, its new imperial master.

It is now acting to preserve the military and economic interests of its master state. This is encapsulated in the AUKUS war pact, which, despite no public debate, commits the country to eight nuclear-powered submarines, high-tech weapons development and sharing and the subsequent invasion of US personnel and weaponry in the event of our “interoperability” in a contrived future conflict with China.

Through AUKUS, Australia acts as a mechanism for US force projection into the Pacific, to rattle the sabre against China.

AUKUS makes Australia the first non-nuclear-weapons state to use a loophole in the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons for naval propulsion with weapons-grade uranium.

That sets a proliferation precedent.

Climate change is the real security threat. Pacific leaders named climate change their main security threat in the 2018 Boe Declaration. Yet Australia keeps expanding fossil fuel exports while spending hundreds of billions on submarines.

But AUKUS is about so much more than submarines; its more sinister part is AUKUS Pillar II, which is about “advanced capabilities” including: undersea capabilities; quantum science; artificial intelligence (AI) and autonomy; advanced cyber; hypersonics and counter-hypersonics; and electronic warfare.

Any pretense about “defensive” capabilities is put to rest with Pillar II because these technologies are about highly efficient offensive war-fighting capabilities.

The Australian Human Rights Commission said it is arguably impossible for AI to comply with the proportionality rule, because AI is unable to understand the intrinsic value of human life.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres said that machines determining proportionality in life-or-death situations is “politically unacceptable and morally repugnant”.

Australia said in 2018 that it was premature to regulate Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems. Nearly a decade later, it maintains this position despite significant advances and uses of the technology.

It is instead barrelling ahead with developing the most advanced and lethal forms imaginable.

The first “signature project” of AUKUS Pillar II was announced in May — payloads and systems for uncrewed undersea vehicles are due from 2027, covering surveillance, reconnaissance, strike, anti-submarine and electronic warfare, among other missions.

The stated aim is meeting near-term war fighting objectives. The Ghost Shark project for Australia is being developed by Silicon Valley-based defence contractor Anduril. Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy said they will conduct surveillance and can strike at extremely long distances. It means the weapon is designed to operate far from our shores — not for defence.

Pillar II extends into the realms of software and artificial intelligence. Tests for active warfighting scenarios to integrate Australian, British and US AI models have been ongoing for years.

A 2023 pilot had Australia PA-8 Poseidon aircraft sharing data for submarine detection, amid other tests of “AI-enabled assets” and machine-learning models.

There was a large-scale US trial in 2024. The US Department of War was enthusiastic: “These trials demonstrated significant progress since the first AUKUS RAAIT trails in the UK in April 2023 and show tangible results of the AUKUS Pillar II commitment to making our warfighter more lethal on the battlefield.

“It used to be that each nation used its own datasets to develop separate models and deploy those models on their own platforms. Under RAAIT, we’ve matured the AI pipeline, focusing on interchangeability and interoperability, which allows for any combinations of datasets, models, algorithms and platforms to be used across all three nations.”

These models and cloud computational capacity are key to war power investments today.

The Pentagon’s AI office awarded Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and xAI contracts worth up to US$200 million each for military and intelligence AI last year.

title: Emon Azmi - Solidarity has to have teeth
content:
Author

: Emon Azmi

Title

: Solidarity has to have teeth

Subtitle

: Where’s the anti-imperialism that goes beyond lip service in the west?

Source

: https://thatanarkatamuslim.substack.com/p/solidarity-has-to-have-teeth


 A recent

Open Letter to Iran’s Political Prisoners

 published by the Guardian has gotten lots of attention (criticism and defense). i have some thoughts on this. However, i’m more interested in discussing an ongoing anti-anarchism issue within the western ‘anti-imperialist’ sphere. Let’s get into it.


(Note: the title is a quote from F12 in a recent


interview


with The Dugout)


On the Guardian letter (kinda)


 That the Islamic Republic of Iran is, de facto, an anti-imperial State in our present international context is not a question. That carcerality is a defining feature of modern States, a core colonial-imperial infrastructure exported from and upheld to an outsized degree by the west (especially the US and Israel), is not a question. That the Guardian letter does not properly articulate this — that it does not offer a constructive analysis of the resulting tensions nor a useful outlook for anti-carceral international solidarity, insofar as revolutionary internationalism is concerned — is clear. There is no need to defend the letter or its signatories on these points.


 It is, however, frustrating that many segments of the western left are sooner jumping to defend the anti-imperial position of the Islamic Republic than to clarify how their anti-imperialist praxis contends with carcerality across contexts and present an alternative anti-carceral outlook within their critique. It’s even more frustrating that this is so unsurprising.


 The sib X, from

HoodSchoolNYC

, hit the nail on the head when they

penned this

:


I think a lot of the western left, and right for that matter, engages politics like sports teams mascots. There’s a certain decadence to an “anti imperialism” that never requires a drop of your blood — only statements, open letters and unfounded audacity… It’s all so unserious. Safiya Bukhari said,

 “it could be that, after all, we don’t want the same things”

, maybe that is true. What frustrates me most is that despite freedom dreams or slogans, the proverbial big bad wolf of imperialism sleeps peacefully each night in the house we all live in.


 The evident lack of substantive anti-imperialism in the west — that is, the kind which would position progressive and anti-war forces against empire’s existence in their ‘internationalist’ practice — is telling. Where is the

solidarity with teeth

 so needed in this moment?


 At present, ‘anti-imperialism’ in the west largely amounts to sectarian navel gazing, sideline cheering, and moral posturing of the sort we see in the Guardian letter.


 ‘Narrative war’ is waged between factions of leftists in a virtual ‘marketplace of ideas’ in a propaganda economy that metabolizes their open letters and statements — fueling their hostilities and feeding off their content, rendering the bulk of their interventions materially insignificant, relegating them to silos in our current media ecosystem. Here, ‘anti-imperialism’ is largely assessed by one’s rhetorical fealty to whatever stance or analysis their niche of leftists has deemed correct. “Hollow”, ironically, characterizes this all quite well.


 Criticisms can be pointed at the individuals, groups, media outlets, and social media accounts comprising these factions — many, justifiably so. But at what point does this counterproductive form of practice itself receive greater scrutiny?


 At what point do insights from those who have been naming the issues of this approach to ‘solidarity’, analyzing the conditions from which it emerges and the forces perpetuating it, get foregrounded? At what point will the work of developing material bases of power at the grassroots level become the primary site from which revolutionary internationalism is conceptualized and discussed, specifically among ‘anti-imperialists’ in the west?


 To these ends, non-statist and anti-statist frameworks (e.g. anarchism, autonomism) have great value. But a pervasive left anti-anarchism is blurring this reality.

The Statism Inherent to Fascism


discusses this further)

title: In the Public Eye: “Albert Einstein’s ‘Why Socialism?'”
content:
London Review of Books

: Letters section features a quote from  John Bellamy Foster’s introduction to the book:


“…Einstein’s essay ‘Why Socialism?’, published in 1949 in the first issue of

Monthly Review

, remains one of the most succinct and powerful arguments for socialism ever written. ‘The crippling of the social consciousness,’ Einstein wrote, is ‘the worst evil of capitalism’. ‘I am convinced’, he concluded, ‘there is only one way to eliminate these grave evils, namely through the establishment of a socialist economy.’


‘Why Socialism?’ was regarded by the FBI as direct confirmation of what they referred to as Einstein’s strong ‘communist sympathies’. The Bureau had opened a file on him in late 1932, when he was in the US on a visitor’s visa to teach at Caltech, with a long report by the Woman Patriot Corporation arguing that he should not be admitted to the country. ‘Not even Stalin himself,’ the WPC charged, ‘is affiliated with so many anarcho-communist international groups to promote … world revolution and ultimate anarchy, as ALBERT EINSTEIN.’ The FBI continued to collect everything it could on Einstein’s socialist connections for the remainder of his life.”


As the U.S. approached its 250th anniversary, the current US President respectively imprisoned and killed the heads of Venezuela and Iran in a clear attempt to control access to their oil supplies. It then found itself mired in another imperialist war in the Middle East that is very likely to veer towards World War III. Einstein’s perspective links alienation and nuclear annihilation, capitalism to the devastating possibility of omnicide — the destruction of all human life on earth.


Einstein’s prescient article “Why Socialism?”, first published by Monthly Review in its inaugural 1949 issue, has to say the least, been circulating for some time. Yet it has never been more relevant than today.

Monthly Review Magazine

 republished the article online in 2009, making the article even more widely available.

Monthly Review Press

‘ recent reprint,

‘Albert Einstein’s “Why Socialism?”‘

 stands out, however, for the extremely enlightening and thorough introduction written by magazine editor, John Bellamy Foster.

In defiance of those who would like to, not only re-write history, but erase the future, please help us get this book out to as wide an audience as possible.


In the Public Eye


One of the many places you can find this classic essay, which just happens to be more relevant now than perhaps at any time in history.

Pictured here at Labyrinth in Princeton.


GPEnewsdocs, with Lynn Fries:


In the last segment of an interview series on ecology and materialism conducted by journalist Lynn Fries, John Bellamy Foster reflects on the enduring relevance of Einstein’s “Why Socialism?”. Marx’s foundations of ecological materialism are blended with the work of natural scientists and the Greek philosopher Epicurus. Socialism, as a transformational project whose intellectual birthplace is materialism, had to be forcefully defended by Albert Einstein, the preeminent scientist of the 20th century. Bellamy Foster, discussing his Introduction to Einstein’s essay, explains the importance of Einstein’s contribution in the postwar context and into the present.

author: Publicación Abierta
title: Venezuela: En las Comunas permanece viva la reserva estratégica de la Revolución
content:
Venezuela


La hora de los hornos: el internacionalismo en tiempos difíciles


Cira Pascual Marquina (*)


En Venezuela, los internacionalistas deben dirigir su mirada hacia las comunas, porque es allí donde permanece viva la reserva estratégica de la revolución.


Por más de dos décadas, fue fácil solidarizarse con la Revolución Bolivariana. Caracas llegó a ser una suerte de capital política para una izquierda internacional heterogénea: militantes de partido y sindicalistas, antiimperialistas e intelectuales y, cada vez más, personas cuya relación con la política estaba mediada por las redes sociales. Llegaban a congresos, reuniones y elecciones. Eran hospedados en hoteles de lujo, se reunían con funcionarios del gobierno y, en algunos casos, con comuneros y activistas de base. Luego, regresaban a casa llevando consigo las imágenes y los argumentos de una revolución que, durante gran parte de ese período, avanzaba a pesar de la tremenda presión que el imperialismo ejercía sobre el proceso.


Esta historia es importante. Venezuela abrió un espacio político y material en el que gentes de diferentes partes del mundo pudieron reunirse, intercambiar experiencias e imaginar un proyecto común. Los encuentros internacionales organizados durante los años de Chávez y Maduro formaron parte de un esfuerzo más amplio por construir una nueva geografía política en América Latina y el Sur Global. Colaboraron para mantener redes, amistades, campañas y formas de cooperación política que de otro modo habrían sido difíciles de establecer. Sería mezquino e históricamente inexacto desestimar estas experiencias simplemente porque las condiciones que las hicieron posibles han cambiado desde entonces, o porque algunos visitantes se sintieron atraídos tanto por los privilegios que les otorgó la revolución como por la tarea de construirla.


Había, sin embargo, un techo para esta forma de solidaridad. Las condiciones materiales permitían participar en la revolución sin compartir sus riesgos o las crecientes dificultades cotidianas que enfrentadas por los venezolanos del pueblo trabajador a causa del bloqueo imperialista. El propio gobierno lo hizo posible: mediante un gran esfuerzo de organización y sacrificio colectivo, desarrolló la capacidad de recibir a miles de visitantes, organizar eventos y proporcionar alojamiento, permitiendo así que el visitante internacionalista viviera la revolución sin verse afectado por las penurias que pasaban los venezolanos y, a menudo, al margen de los intensos debates que se desarrollaban en las bases. Este internacionalismo exigía poco de quienes lo practicaban y ofrecía recompensas a los visitantes, pero fue útil.


La situación ha cambiado drásticamente. Desde el 3 de enero, cuando el imperialismo estadounidense bombardeó objetivos en Venezuela y secuestró al presidente Nicolás Maduro y a la diputada Cilia Flores, el Proceso Bolivariano ha entrado en un período mucho más difícil, marcado por retrocesos tácticos, nuevas contradicciones y acontecimientos que han restringido algunas de los caminos abiertos por la revolución. Por ahora, no se trata de un simple retroceso, sino de una vuelta atrás que cierra ciertas posibilidades, mientras deja intacto el terreno sobre el cual continúa el proceso radical de construcción de comunas.


Para muchos internacionalistas que viajaron a Venezuela antes del 3 de enero, el proyecto comunal estaba, en gran medida, al margen de su participación política con la revolución, aunque muchos realizaron visitas de dos o tres horas a alguna comuna de Caracas. Sin embargo, el discurso en torno a la comuna se convirtió en un pilar central de la defensa internacional de la Revolución Bolivariana. Este énfasis no fue infundado. Hoy, las comunas constituyen la principal reserva estratégica de la revolución, aunque su desarrollo sigue siendo altamente desigual.


El proceso revolucionario venezolano no ha llegado a su fin. La experiencia política acumulada durante más de dos décadas permanece viva en muchas comunas, así como las capacidades forjadas a través de años de lucha. Y, quizás más importante aún, las comunas continúan existiendo como espacios vivos de resistencia, organización, producción, deliberación y poder popular, aunque con niveles muy diferentes de desarrollo y conciencia política.


En su mejor expresión, el internacionalismo es una relación de compromiso político recíproca –aunque no necesariamente simétrico– entre fuerzas organizadas: un intercambio de capacidades …

Progressive groups led by the Bagong Alvansang Makabayan (Bayan) and International League of Peoples Struggle (ILPS) Philippines on Thursday expressed their strong condemnation as the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC) Investment Forum inaugurated on Thursday, September 10 at the Grand Hyatt Hotel at the Bonifacio Global City, Taguig City.

The group said the initiative is a threat to Philippine sovereignty and a vehicle for foreign control over the country’s resources.

In a joint statement, the groups rejected the LEC, calling it a “massive sellout” of Philippine patrimony, and accused the government of allowing foreign interests to shape the country’s infrastructure and economic development agenda.

Sponsored by the U.S. Trade and Development Agency (USTDA), the event brought together about 600 international investors, industry leaders, project developers, and government officials to discuss investment opportunities within the Subic-Clark-Manila-Batangas corridor.

Bayan and ILPS argued that the corridor would not lead to genuine industrialization but instead create profit opportunities for foreign companies and local business interests. The groups questioned the prominent role of the U.S. government in promoting the initiative, noting that the USTDA is sponsoring and organizing the investment forum

According to the USTDA, the LEC is a trilateral initiative involving the Philippines, the United States, and Japan aimed at mobilizing investments in transportation, logistics, energy, digital infrastructure, and advanced manufacturing. The agency said the corridor seeks to strengthen connectivity and economic growth across Luzon

The groups also cited the proposed 232-kilometer Subic-Clark-Manila-Batangas Freight Railway, which they said would primarily serve foreign commercial interests. Corridor documents identify the freight railway as a key transport project linking major economic hubs in Luzon.

Among the projects criticized by the groups was the proposed Pax Silica Economic Security Zone, which they claimed could accelerate critical mineral extraction and affect Indigenous and agricultural communities.

Bayan and ILPS further alleged that the corridor forms part of a broader U.S. strategy in the Indo-Pacific and raised concerns over what they described as the possible dual-use nature of infrastructure projects located near strategic transportation and military facilities.

The groups said several corridor projects could support both commercial and defense-related activities, citing developments in Subic and other strategic locations. Corridor materials show that the LEC connects key economic centers, ports, airports, and transport networks across Subic, Clark, Manila, and Batangas.

Bayan and ILPS urged the public to reject the corridor, arguing that national development should remain under Filipino control and not be driven by foreign governments or investors. The groups also criticized recent government policies that they said were designed to attract more foreign investment and expand critical mineral projects associated with the corridor.

“Do not sell the Philippines to foreigners. The Philippines belongs to Filipinos. If the government is to undertake projects or programs for industrialization, these should be geared toward national industrialization by Filipinos and for Filipinos, not for foreign interests.,” said former Bayan Muna Rep. Teddy Casino, now chairperson of Bayan, during the protest.

For Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP), the LEC is being presented as “economic development” by Ferdinand Marcos administration, but in reality, the group said it is “really a corridor for imperialist profit and war.”

“Filipino land, resources and infrastructure are being prepared to serve foreign corporations, global supply chains and the strategic military interests of the United States,” said KMP Chairperson Danilo ‘Ka Daning’ Ramos in a statement.

author: Editors
title: 9/11: How the US turned tragedy into barbarity
content:
Twenty-five years ago, the world changed irrevocably. Not because terrorists from the al-Qaeda network attacked the United States, bringing down the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers in New York, hitting the Pentagon in Virginia and killing nearly 3,000 people. It changed because of US imperialism’s response.

The day after 9/11, the editors of

Socialist Alternative

 magazine, one of the precursor publications of

Red Flag

, warned: “The real threat to people around the world is not terrorism, but the racism, militarism, repression and nationalism that has been unleashed in the wake of the terrorist attacks”.

A week later, President George W. Bush, in an address to a joint session of Congress, announced his so-called War on Terror: “Every nation, in every region, now has a decision to make. Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists”. His administration rode the wave of outrage over al-Qaeda’s assault to open a new era of imperialist aggression that has cost millions of people’s lives. 

First came Afghanistan in October. It didn’t matter that the ruling Taliban

offered to hand over Osama bin Laden

, the alleged mastermind of the terrorist attacks, to a neutral country to face trial. The US was interested only in war. Condoleezza Rice, then Bush’s national security adviser, admitted as much to the

New Yorker

’s Nicholas Lemann several months later. In the wake of the 9/11 attacks, she had asked senior national security staff to think about how to “capitalise on these opportunities”. 

The Bush administration soon began making a public case for invading Iraq—which had no ties to 9/11—declaring the country part of an “axis of evil” with Iran and North Korea. Undersecretary of State John Bolton soon expanded the axis list to include Cuba, Libya and Syria. The bombs started raining down on Baghdad in March 2003.

These invasions would have been followed by more had the resistance in Iraq not bogged down the US military in an intractable counterinsurgency. Nevertheless, Brown University’s

Costs of War research

 estimates the direct death toll from US military operations in the post-9-11 era in Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, Yemen and Pakistan to be close to 1 million people. It estimates a further 3.6 to 3.8 million “indirect” deaths resulting from the “destruction of economies, healthcare systems, infrastructure and the environment”. 

The US also set up a global kidnapping network, which it termed “extraordinary rendition”, and a series of “black sites” in which prisoners were held without charge and tortured.

The Open Society Foundation estimates

 that 54 governments collaborated in the program. Then there is the notorious

Guantánamo Bay torture camp

, used since 2002 and still holding ageing prisoners from the War on Terror. This all served as notice that the US empire would stop at nothing to maintain its global domination.

A more enduring legacy of this era of “forever wars” has been the construction of vast internal security and surveillance states, which have trampled civil and democratic rights. 

More than 140 governments have adopted “counterterrorism” legislation since 9/11, beginning with the USA PATRIOT Act, which green-lit mass surveillance and delayed-notice search warrants and bolstered spy agency resources. Mega-departments, such as Homeland Security in the US and Home Affairs in Australia, were established as Western states have become more authoritarian.

Indeed, Australia is one of the worst offenders. “No other nation can match the volume of Australia’s counter-terrorism laws”, wrote legal academics Rebecca Ananian-Welsh and Keiran Hardy in

a 2021 piece for the University of Queensland’s

Contact

 magazine

. They describe the scope of the laws as “staggering”, “unprecedented” and “extreme”, noting that they go beyond even “historical wartime powers”.

They include control orders, preventive detention, and compulsory retention of all telecommunication and online data of every resident. The

Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Act

 of 2021 gave law enforcement agencies the power to take control of a person’s individual online accounts, modify or delete their data and even take over entire networks. That is, they can legally alter a person’s text messages.

Death and destruction abroad and authoritarianism at home: such is the “rules-based order”, the purported demise of which we are supposed to lament. This post-9/11 era normalised authoritarianism …

author: gavroche
title: Ceuta muestra el futuro
content:
Encontrado en

Valladolor


En 

el frente externo

 el ataque por parte de Marruecos a la frontera española es el enésimo movimiento en una pugna cada vez menos soterrada entre las potencias imperialistas (la primera de ellas, España) por el control del apetecible bocado que es el norte de África, de Libia a Mauritania. La utilización de decenas de miles de migrantes como carne de cañón en el frente da cuenta de la verdadera magnitud del conflicto: masas de desheredados, desposeídas hasta de lo más mínimo, maltratadas durante meses en las montañas de la frontera o traídas como ganado desde los pueblos rifeños, son lanzadas, al precio de decenas de muertos -contabilizados sólo en el momento de cruzar la frontera-, como una especie de batallón de la miseria contra el que se espera que se descarguen los primeros golpes del enemigo.


En la jerga militar moderna se habla de 

guerra híbrida

 para referirse a los movimientos hostiles que no se desarrollan sobre el campo de batalla tradicional, pero el nombre no debe esconder qué realidad hay detrás: es un episodio más en el camino hacia el enfrentamiento militar que tarde o temprano llegará.


No tendrá por qué ser entre Marruecos y España, países que a fin de cuentas son socios entre sí y, al mismo tiempo, socios de la gran potencia norteamericana -más que probablemente, la fuerza que está detrás de estos sucesos-, pero sí entre algunas de las fuerzas imperialistas que pelean por cada terreno en el mundo. Seguramente, el Magreb no sea uno de estos terrenos que se sitúan directamente en disputa, pero desde luego juega un papel de catalizador de otros enfrentamientos de mayor escala. En cualquier caso, el resultado inmediato es visible para todo el mundo. No se trata sólo de que se incremente la hostilidad contra Marruecos, porque esta es una reacción inducida, cuyo fin no es tanto el odio al vecino del sur sino extender a través de ello un sentimiento nacionalista generalizado, basado por supuesto en el odio a todos los rivales nacionales de la burguesía española. Se trata, pues, de un primer episodio de movilización nacionalista y militarista en un país como España, para el que ni el Medio Oriente ni Ucrania son motivos suficientes como para la movilización bélica, donde hasta ahora no había tenido lugar.


Se equivocan -interesadamente o no- quienes pretenden minimizar el problema reduciéndolo a algún tipo de “crisis migratoria” o problema de tipo humanitario. Los miles de migrantes lanzados sobre Ceuta son carne de cañón en una estrategia bélica. Nuestra solidaridad, la solidaridad de clase que el proletariado debe levantar como única respuesta ante quienes quieren hacerles pasar por “invasores”, no va dirigida a ellos en cuanto simples migrantes, sino como víctimas de una movilización militarista que se debe combatir en ambos lados de la frontera, pero sobre todo desde España donde el proletariado debe rechazar toda llamada a la solidaridad nacional contra Marruecos, todo discurso de país agredido que se defiende del agresor y, en fin, todo intento de utilizar este incidente como un paso más en la pendiente nacionalista y militarista que anima gustosa la burguesía española.


Hoy es la “Ceuta agredida”, mañana será la integridad de cualquier socio de la OTAN que se vea comprometida en Medio Oriente, Europa del Este o Asia… España forma parte de un entramado de relaciones y alianzas interimperialistas impuestas por las potencias vencedoras de la IIª Guerra Mundial, con Estados Unidos a la cabeza, que hoy está puesto en cuestión por el crecimiento de otras potencias imperialistas, fuerzas antes menores que hoy ya son una amenaza al dominio norteamericano. En esa situación se enmarca tanto el episodio de Ceuta del pasado julio como la respuesta dada por todas las fuerzas de la burguesía española: con él se llama a la defensa de la “españolidad” de la ciudad, como vía para una movilización nacionalista de más amplio alcance, que se manifestará con mucha más fuerza en futuras ocasiones en las que los intereses del imperialismo español, directa o indirectamente, se pongan en riesgo.


	En 

el frente interno

, han aparecido todas las escorias del sistema: las bandas ultra nacionalistas que recorren la ciudad a la caza del inmigrante, los grupos fascistas que han desembarcado en Ceuta a lo largo de estas semanas para participar en los pogromos, el ejército -con sus nada disimulados soldados de paisano- y la inteligencia militar, dirigiendo con tácticas militares las …

author: Unknown
title: Elia Ayoub - Actually Existing Multipolarity
content:
Author

: Elia Ayoub

Title

: Actually Existing Multipolarity

Date

: 29 April 2026

Source

: “The I.B. Tauris Handbook of Authoritarianism in the Arab World”, 2026


Introduction


 Since the 2011 Syrian revolution and the 2014 Euromaidan in Ukraine, many Syrians and Ukrainians have found themselves sharing a common enemy: Russian imperialism. Russia’s intervention in Syria started at the end of 2015, over a year after Russia first invaded Ukraine and annexed Crimea. Since then, Russian forces have bombed large parts of Syria to allow Bashar al-Assad and his Iranian and Iran-backed allies to maintain power until his overthrow in December of 2024. At the same time, since 2014 but especially since February 2022, Russia has been waging a genocidal war against Ukraine, with the clear intention, as stated multiple times by Putin and other high-ranking officials,

[1]

 to destroy Ukrainian identity and culture.


 Although the motives behind them differ, the Russian intervention in Syria and invasion of Ukraine have both led to widespread destruction. As a result, a number of Syrians and Ukrainians have found—and worked to build—solidarity with one another. Russia, meanwhile, has redeployed soldiers that were active in Syria to Ukraine and Ukrainian forces have fought Russian forces in Syria, making the link between these two causes even clearer.

[2]

 Syrian aid workers have also volunteered in Ukraine, where they have drawn on their experiences dealing with Russia in their home country.

[3]

 Syrians took to the streets to declare their support for the Ukrainian resistance even before 2022,

[4]

 revealing an understanding that these two countries are now linked. Furthermore, the Assad regime is among the few governments to have recognized Russian-annexed Ukrainian territories as Russian,

[5]

 and Iranian weapons are being used in Russia’s ongoing campaign against Ukraine.

[6]


 Despite that, most Ukrainians remain seemingly uneducated about the Syrian struggle against the axis of Assad, Russia, and Iran beyond the knowledge of this mutual enemy. Furthermore, the difference in how Europe has received Ukrainian refugees versus how it has received Syrian refugees has led many to believe, understandably so, that the Ukrainian cause is valued in Europe while the Syrian one is not. This was worsened by racist European media coverage of Syrian refugees, especially when compared to coverage of Ukrainian refugees.

[7]

 In this chapter, I will explore how Ukrainians’ experience with Russian imperialism can serve as a bridge to other anti-imperialist struggles, and how arguments in favor of multipolarity fail to take into account similarities between authoritarian forces that nominally oppose one another—in other words, actually existing multipolarity. Instead, the experience of struggles on the peripheries suggests that, as with Ukrainians and Syrians, bond-building between victims of imperialism can help pave the way for truly anti-imperialist politics.


“Our Wounds Are Bridges”


 In 2022, I moderated a four-way panel featuring two Ukrainians and two Syrians as part of the “Post-Extractive Futures” series organized by War on Want, Tipping Point UK, JunteGente, and The Fire These Times.

[8]

 On the Ukrainian side were Yuliya Yurchenko, a senior lecturer and researcher in political economy at the University of Greenwich and the author of

Ukraine and the Empire of Capital

, and Taras Bilous, a historian, activist with the Social Movement organization, and editor for

Commons: Journal of Social Criticism

, covering war and nationalism. Bilous was also fighting on the front lines at the time of the conversation. On the Syrian side were Yassin al-Haj Saleh—a writer and former political prisoner, as well as the husband of Samira al-Khalil, a famed feminist activist who was abducted by the armed Islamist group Jaysh Al-Islam in Douma in December 2013—and Wafa Mustafa, an activist and detention survivor whose father was forcibly disappeared by the Assad regime in 2013. The conversation was recorded on YouTube

[9]

, and a transcription has been made available by Antidote Zine Collective.

[10]


 The title of the roundtable set the tone for the topic: “Our Wounds Are Bridges: The Threads that Bind Us from Syria to Ukraine.” The intention of the organizers, as stated in the announcement, was to provide “a space for mutual learning and solidarity-weaving amongst activists dreaming, enacting and mobilising toward …

author: Daron Letts
title: Northern construction leaders call for more housing, local trades training
content:
Four big players in Nunavut’s construction industry achieved consensus within moments of the start of the “Builders Behind our Communities” panel Wednesday at the Nunavut Trade Show in Iqaluit.


“Execution without capacity-building is not OK,” is how Arctic Fresh general manager Evan Schellenberg summed it up. He was one of four panelists who discussed how construction companies are involved in the communities where they build.


Schellenberg pointed out that even many of the delegates in the audience slept on couches the night before.


“Every project must be seen as a housing project,” he said. “It can’t be a side note.”


The annual Nunavut Trade Show, which started Monday, gives business leaders a chance to meet and discuss ideas during four days of panel discussions, speeches and workshops.


While eyes across Canada are looking North with Ottawa spending billions to expand the country’s military presence in the Arctic, Nunavut’s housing crisis

continues to worsen

. Twenty communities have a “critical” housing need, according the Nunavut Housing Corporation’s 2024-25 annual report.


Meanwhile, in Iqaluit, new housing is

not keeping up

 with demand, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation said in its Northern Housing Report, released earlier this year. Iqaluit’s vacancy rate is 0.3 per cent, the report found.


Water, sewer, and power infrastructure likewise should not be approached as afterthoughts, added Tower Arctic Ltd. managing director Gordon Paterson, during the panel.


Others expressed a need to train an Inuit workforce at home.


“We need to look at how we can support, train and develop members of the community,” said Carleigh Bell, director of pursuits and pre-construction for EllisDon Corp.


That involves establishing trades training right where people live, without pulling individuals away for apprenticeship programs far from their support networks, she said.


Stephanie Li, chief financial officer for Birchcliff Development Ltd., agreed.


“We are trying hard to train the local Inuit so they can build for their own,” Li said.


The speakers also called on the Government of Nunavut to involve Inuit tradespeople in its tendering process as early as possible.


Doing so would enhance opportunities for them from Day One and furnish companies with local knowledge early in the construction process, the panelists said.

„

Artikel 1 GG: “Die Würde aller Menschen, die über ein mittleres oder hohes Einkommen verfügen, ist unantastbar”. Kommt Ihnen an diesem Satz etwas merkwürdig vor? Richtig: Eigentlich heißt es: “Die Würde des Menschen” – aller Menschen. Da ja niemand so gemein wäre, die zuständigen Behörden und die Stromlieferanten des Verfassungsbruchs zu bezichtigen, können wir daraus nur eine Schlussfolgerung ziehen: Personen, die es aus sozialer Not heraus nicht mehr schaffen, ihren Strom zu bezahlen, sind überhaupt keine Menschen. Denn ist es etwa “würdig”, ohne warmes Wasser und warme Mahlzeiten zu leben, ohne Telefon, Internet, Radio und Fernsehen, mit ungebügelter Wäsche, frierend und im Dunkeln? In Anlehung an Marie Antoinette könnte man da vielleicht raten: “Wenn sie keinen Strom mehr haben, sollen sie halt Kerzen aufstellen!” Holdger Platta weist in seinem erschütternden und hervorragend recherchierten Artikel auf einen alltäglichen Skandal hin, der selbst in “linken” und sozial engagierten Kreisen viel zu selten, viel zu wenig vehement kritisiert wird

author: CMI Argentina
title: Neuquén: la provincia le dio la personería jurídica a la comunidad Melo pero sigue la amenaza de desalojo
content:
En Neuquén el gobierno provincial acaba de reconocer la personería jurídica a la Lof Melo. Lo paradójico de esta situación es que la reconoce la personería jurídica como comunidad, sin embargo la amenaza de desalojo no retrocede.


Escuchá el reporte de Maitén Cañicul desde la FM Che.


Julieta Melo, werquen de la Lof Melo, expresó al respecto: “El gobierno nos otorgó la personería jurídica y con este acto se cerró la discusión. Este conflicto no es un conflicto entre privados” y agregó que “la personería jurídica es el DNI colectivo de una comunidad mapuche, algo que viene negando sistemáticamente el juez Bonorino y la terrateniente Cristina Broers a través de su abogado Guillermo Hensel”.


“No necesitábamos estos papeles para demostrar nuestra existencia colectiva como comunidad, pero sabemos que en este sistema era la evidencia con la que podíamos tirar por la borda esa persistente postura negacionista”, explicó.


Los seis consejos zonales de la Confederación Mapuche en Neuquén presentaron una nota a Rolando Figueroa, gobernador de la provincia y al ministro Jorge Tobares, solicitando la personería jurídica no sólo a la comunidad Melo sino también a otras comunidades que la vienen reclamando hace bastante tiempo: “Instamos al gobierno de la provincia del Neuquén el otorgamiento inmediato de personerías jurídicas a todas las comunidades mapuche que la están demandando”.


Además solicitaban la intervención urgente del gobierno de Neuquén ante el fallo injusto del juez Bonorino que mantiene bajo grave amenaza a la comunidad Melo: “La situación de un inminente desalojo no ha cesado, generando una carga emocional sobre mi comunidad. Nos llevará mucho tiempo reparar todo el daño ya causado, por eso el acompañamiento que estamos teniendo hace mucho más llevadera esta situación”.


“Sabemos que si el juez Bonorino mantiene esta postura negacionista y racista hacia nuestra lof y pretende llevar adelante este desalojo, estos acompañamientos se van a multiplicar por todo el territorio”, agregó.

con

author: anred
title: Otra vez la amenaza de desalojo a comunidades mapuche en las Lof Melo y Kinxikew
content:
Foto: Pilar Mateos


La Justicia neuquina volvió a avanzar con el desalojo de las comunidades mapuche Lof Melo y Lof Kinxikew, en el paraje El Pedregoso, entre Villa La Angostura y Bariloche. Mientras permanece pendiente la ejecución de la medida, la Confederación Mapuche de Neuquén reclamó al gobernador Rolando Figueroa que intervenga para detenerla. Tambièn, el propio Gobierno provincial reconoció este viernes la personería jurídica del Lof Melo, después de 14 años de trámite. Por ANRed


La nueva amenaza surge luego del operativo del 19 de agosto, cuando efectivos de la Policía de Neuquén y del grupo especial GEOP ingresaron al territorio para ejecutar una orden judicial. En aquella jornada fue desalojada una parte del predio recuperada por integrantes del Lof Melo. El procedimiento quedó inconcluso cuando las fuerzas debían avanzar sobre otro sector donde se encontraban menores y no estaban presentes funcionarios de organismos de protección de la infancia. Ahora, el juez Francisco Astoul Bonorino libró un nuevo mandamiento para completar el desalojo del sector donde permanecen integrantes del Lof Kinxikew. La medida todavía no tiene fecha de ejecución pero las cominidades ya anunciaron que permanecen en alerta y movilizados. En aquella fecha, una multitud se acercò para solidarizarse y logrò la suspensiòn del desalojo.


La nueva orden judicial vuelve a colocar a las comunidades en estado de alerta. El conflicto se desarrolla sobre un predio de unas 625 hectáreas atravesado por la Ruta Nacional 40, en el paraje El Pedregoso. El expediente se inició en 2011 y la denuncia por usurpación fue presentada en 2012 por María Cristina Broers, quien sostiene ser propietaria del inmueble desde 1969. Con el paso de los años, integrantes de la familia Quintriqueo se incorporaron a la recuperaciòn de su ancestral territorio y conformaron el Lof Kinxikew. Distintas instancias judiciales mantuvieron la orden de restitución del inmueble.


Pero para las comunidades y la Confederación Mapuche el conflicto no puede reducirse a una disputa entre particulares. Los Consejos Zonales reclamaron al gobernador Figueroa una intervención urgente y señalaron que el territorio del Lof Melo fue relevado como

Ocupación Tradicional y Pública (OTP)

. También cuestionaron que la comunidad haya tenido que atravesar durante años el trámite para obtener su personería jurídica.


La situación suma ahora un elemento particularmente significativo:

el 11 de septiembre, un día después de que se conociera el nuevo mandamiento de desalojo, el Gobierno de Neuquén reconoció oficialmente la personería jurídica del Lof Melo

. El Decreto 1402/2026 sostiene que la comunidad cumple con los requisitos establecidos por la Constitución Nacional y Provincial, el Convenio 169 de la OIT, la Ley 23.302 y demás normativa vigente, y reconoce su domicilio en el paraje Paso Coihue, departamento Los Lagos.


La Confederación Mapuche sostiene que el reconocimiento llega después de

14 años de trámites

, y reclama que esa nueva situación sea considerada en el expediente de desalojo. En una comunicación dirigida al gobernador, las autoridades mapuche advirtieron sobre la gravedad de ejecutar una medida de estas características y reclamaron que la Provincia intervenga para evitar una nueva avanzada policial.


Mientras tanto, la Justicia mantiene abierta la posibilidad de completar el operativo. La nueva orden está dirigida principalmente al sector donde permanece el Lof Kinxikew, luego de que en agosto la Policía avanzara sobre la fracción ocupada por el Lof Melo. La ejecución aún no tiene fecha, pero el mandamiento ya fue librado.

author: Nahuel Lag
title: El modelo Arauco en Misiones: amenazas, detenciones y casas quemadas con complicidad estatal
content:
Por Clarisa Néztor


Puerto Argentino 1, 2 y 3, Palmera Boca y San Juan Bosco son parajes rurales del municipio de San Pedro, en el nordeste de Misiones. La Comisión Vecinos Unidos por las Chacras reúne en esos parajes a cerca de 200 familias que producen alimentos en pequeñas parcelas para sostener sus economías.

Desde hace años sufren una persecución sistemática de violencia institucional y un hostigamiento permanente por parte de la forestal Arauco,

 que los acusa de ocupar tierras a pesar de no presentar cargos formales ante el Poder Judicial. En las últimas semanas, la violencia escaló con una represión cuyo objetivo fue sembrar el terror y forzar a las familias a abandonar sus chacras. “Ni Arauco, ni el gobierno municipal ni el provincial nos mostraron un título de propiedad”, sostiene Diego Antúnez, productor y presidente de la comisión de vecinos a quien le incendiaron su casa a fines de agosto.   


Los productores describen cómo el personal de Arauco, acompañado por la Policía de Misiones, ingresa a las chacras sin órdenes de desalojo, realiza amenazas, detenciones y prende fuego las viviendas de madera. Las denuncias de las familias campesinas fueron públicas y radicadas ante el Poder Judicial de San Pedro. Las personas perjudicadas exigen la respuesta del gobernador de Misiones, Hugo Passalacqua, y la regularización de las tierras. 


La situación desatada a mediados de agosto, llevó a los vecinos a mantener varios días de acampe frente al Municipio de San Pedro, donde el intendente Miguel Ángel Dos Santos lleva tres años sin darles respuestas. En Posadas, la comisión de vecinos se reunió en varias oportunidades con Daniel Behler, subsecretario provincial de Tierras y Colonización, quien se comprometió a avanzar con un relevamiento de las familias afectadas, solicitar información sobre el accionar policial denunciado y abrir una mesa de diálogo con Arauco, al que la empresa nunca se presentó.


La última reunión de la comisión de Vecinos Unidos por las Chacras con el subsecretario Behler ocurrió este miércoles. Antúnez contó a

Tierra Viva

 que el funcionario provincial volvió a pedirle a las familias un relevamiento de las chacras en las que producen para poder cruzarlo con la documentación oficial. La comisión de vecinos, que ya había dejado una carpeta con el relevamiento de las chacras, actualizó la información y precisó que son 164 familias que cultivan sus alimentos en 2.300 hectáreas. Sin embargo, no todas las hectáreas son productivas: muchas de ellas mantienen el monte nativo. 


El presidente de la Comisión Vecinos Unidos por las Chacras, Diego Antúnez (izquierda) y una comitiva de familias tras la reunión en la Subsecretaria de Tierras y Colonización. Foto: XR-Misiones


“

Le pedimos (a Behler) la paz. Pedimos que intervengan ante Arauco y la Policía para que cesen con la violencia que están ejerciendo

: el hostigamiento, la persecución, el desalojo arbitrario, la quema de casas. Responsabilizamos al gobierno, directamente, de todo lo que pasó y de lo que va a seguir pasando. El gobierno de Misiones no nos da seguridad y nuestras vidas corren peligro con Arauco”, exigió Antúnez desde Posadas. Allí, junto a una comitiva de colonos, también radicó denuncias ante la Defensoría del Pueblo y la Jefatura de Policía de Misiones. 


La violencia de la empresa forestal recrudeció en espejo con dos normativas tratadas en el Senado nacional con particular interés para Arauco: tras la media sanción de la

“Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada”

 —que mantuvo el capítulo sobre desalojos exprés— y durante el dictamen en el Senado de un proyecto para crear

mercados de carbono

, impulsado por la

Mesa de Carbono Argentina

, integrada por la forestal. 


La multinacional, de capitales chilenos, es

una de los principales propietarios privados de tierras de Misiones

. Está presente en esa provincia desde 1996 y fue adquiriendo hectáreas de plantaciones forestales y áreas naturales por un total aproximadamente 230.000 hectáreas. La vasta extensión territorial está mantiene continuos conflictos por la posesión de la tierra con

familias campesinas

 y

comunidades Mbya Guaraní

, pero el caso de las familias rurales de San Pedro

 se transformó en una emergencia social, habitacional y territorial por los constantes ataques registrados en el último mes

. 


Producir alimentos no es delito

author: Pip Hinman
title: Socialist Alliance candidate says One Nation can be combatted
content:
The following piece is based on Jacob Andrewartha’s speech to an election launch on September 6. He is standing for Socialist Alliance in the Victorian seat of Pascoe Vale.

At the beginning of Israel’s latest genocide in Gaza in October 2023, alongside many other comrades, I helped initiate the first local protest in Coburg for Palestine, which drew more than 1000 people. It helped broaden the movement for Palestine at the local level.

It is inspiring to join people taking action and become more organised against the establishment.

That, after all, is the only way we can counter the rise of One Nation and the neoliberal politics of Labor and the Liberals.

We saw that power with the thousands of high school students who walked out against Pauline Hanson and One Nation earlier last month.

We also saw it at the massive turnout against Israeli Prime Minister Isaac Herzog’s visit to Gadigal Country.

Our collective power is how we push back against capitalist politicians and their billionaire mates.

The rising support for One Nation can be demoralising, just as the Labor Party’s pursuit of right-wing policies.

The only way to combat this is to advance the self-organisation and collective power of working people.

The very conditions that have led to the rise in support for One Nation have to be changed. But that can only change with a fight-back.

The industrial action waged by teachers and education support staff is a recent inspiring example. Their campaign — on the streets — not only pushed the Australian Education Union leadership, it won teachers and support staff a better pay offer from Victorian Labor.

However, while Socialist Alliance is dedicated to building struggles in workplaces and in our communities for concrete demands, this is not enough. We also need to talk about what sort of society we want and how to get it.

The billionaire class is united around their vision — a society where they can continue to enrich themselves from exploiting workers and the Earth. The billionaires won’t stop pushing for low or no taxes on the rich, subsidies and the total privatisation of public services. They also want to continue to drive down wages.

Our vision is one of solidarity. We believe in a society where everyone has the right to housing. We want essential services, like education and healthcare, to be fully funded and resourced. We want real action on the climate emergency. We want fully funded public transport. We want to see a world free of conflict, genocide and oppression.

We want a world where everyone can live their lives to the full — the only way of doing that is if their basic needs are met.

But we have to fight against the ruling class’ marketisation of everything.

Victorian Labor is now considering privatising Melbourne Water. In Britain, such a move led to the return of cholera.

We have to stop Labor from demolishing all 44 high-rise public housing estates and demand it build more public housing. Everyone knows that by leaving housing to the market, the housing affordability crisis will intensify.

We have to fight laws that restrict our ability to protect the rights of working-class people, including restrictions on the right to protest and the right of workers to take industrial action.

Victorian Labor’s plan to destroy the Retail and Fast Food Workers Union (RAFFWU), after having tried to destroy the Construction Forestry and Maritime Employees Union, shows up just how anti-worker it is.

But a society where people’s needs are met and where people can lead fulfilling lives will only be achieved if there is broad support for socialist ideas and solutions. For that, we need a much greater level of self-organisation and preparedness to struggle.

Even without many MPs, One Nation has pressured the establishment parties into adopting parts of its program. Labor has cut temporary visa programs, and it continues to allow refugees to rot on Nauru.

With polls showing a growing alienation from the mainstream parties and many people only relating to politics at election time, Socialist Alliance has to be there to put our vision forward. The far right, and its media supporters, is managing to con people into believing that migration is the cause of the housing crisis, despite the evidence.

Socialist Alliance has been contesting elections since we formed in 2001, because we see the electoral arena as one theatre of struggle to win more people to join the movements for a fairer, more just society …

author: Unknown
title: Iran Human Rights publishes names of over 4,200 people killed in January protests
content:
Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO) has published the names of more than 4,200 people killed during the January 2026 protests in Iran, following months of collecting information, comparing sources, and verifying the identities of victims.


Rojhelat Info

 translated the main findings into English and said that according to the report, at least 420 women and 281 children under the age of 18 are among those identified. Twenty-five of the children were under 14, and the youngest recorded victim was only four and a half months old.


The organization says a large part of the killings took place on January 8 and 9. At least 3,356 people, or 91 percent of the cases where the exact date of death is known, were killed during those two days.


Deaths were documented in cities across 30 of Iran’s 31 provinces. The report also documents repeated patterns of deadly force, including direct fire at protesters, shots aimed at vital parts of the body, shooting people from behind or while they were fleeing, and the use of snipers.


The Iranian authorities have officially announced a death toll of 3,117 people, but Iran Human Rights says the government’s own lists are incomplete. The organization stressed that the figure of more than 4,200 represents only the minimum number of verified deaths and should not be considered the final toll.


Internet shutdowns, pressure on families, restricted access to hospitals and forensic records, and the lack of independent investigations have made it difficult to establish the full scale of the killings.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Groups remember Martial Law with protests
content:
homas Andrei Brecio at Jeoff Larua /Pinoy Weekly

MANILA — “We shall never forget.”

Progressive groups announced on September 15 its planned protest actions on September 21 to commemorate the 54th anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law and to press the government for accountability over corruption, particularly the controversy surrounding flood control projects.

The Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) said that it will join the Kilusang Bayan Kontra Kurakot (KBKK) rally at Liwasang Bonifacio in the afternoon before leading a march to Mendiola.

Bayan said that the mobilization pays tribute to the Filipino people’s resistance to the dictatorship of the late dictator Ferdinand Marcos Sr. while continuing calls for accountability over the flood control controversy that sparked large anti-corruption protests last year.

The group said that the protest should also be a reminder of the continuing problems of poverty, corruption, repression, and foreign influence.

Bayan stressed that the Marcos Sr. dictatorship was marked by state violence, political repression, corruption and cronyism. The Marcos Jr. administration, Bayan said, implemented similar policies through continued political harassment and expanded cooperation with the United States.

The group also criticized the Marcos Jr. administration’s decision to allow US military access to Philippine territory and initiatives such as Pax Silica which it said would integrate Philippine critical-mineral extraction, semiconductor production, energy infrastructure, and artificial intelligence facilities into US-led supply chains.

Beyond the national issues raised by Bayan, sectoral groups are also expected to join the September 21 mobilization, with representatives citing corruption, government spending, environmental destruction, poverty and workers’ concerns.

Jerome Adonis of Kilusang Mayo Uno encouraged workers to be part of the protest as it highlights issues like hunger, poverty, rising prices, and unemployment.

Kedric Calibara, chairperson of the Agham Youth of University of the Philippines-Diliman Engineering, said that engineers and students would participate in the protest as government funds should be used for technological development and public needs.

Calibara cited the reported P174.1 billion allocation for flood control, stressing that government resources should contribute to the country’s technological advancement rather than being lost to corruption.

Environmental concerns will also be part of the mobilization. Nina Fegi of the Panatang Luntian, Environmentalist Stand Against Corruption Alliance raised concerns over mining activities, watershed destruction and government initiatives involving critical minerals.

Fegi criticized the US-Philippines Critical Minerals Memorandum of Understanding and measures intended to accelerate mineral mapping, mining and exploration, arguing that environmental protection is closely connected to addressing flooding. “The best flood control that we can have is when we are able to protect and conserve our mountains and resources.”

Joaquin Buenaflor of Kabataan Partylist said that corruption should not be viewed solely as a problem of individual government officials but as a systemic issue involving the handling of public funds and government projects. Buenaflor called for the return of allegedly stolen public funds and the removal of mechanisms that enable corruption, while urging young people to participate in the mobilization.

Mimi Doringo, secretary-general of the Kalipunan ng Damayang Mahihirap, cited recurring floods, rising prices and low wages as major issues affecting marginalized Filipinos. She called for higher wages and compensation for calamity victims, while urging the government to direct public funds toward social services.

The September 21 protests will also be held in various parts of the country, with groups organizing marches, rallies, forums and multisectoral assemblies in Bicol, Baguio, Iloilo, Roxas City, Aklan, Negros, and Davao City. Activities include marches in Legazpi and Naga, a march-rally from UP Baguio to Malcolm Square, a march to the Ombudsman Regional Office in Iloilo, a march from Roxas City Civic Center to the city plaza, a forum and march in Aklan, a multisectoral assembly and march in Negros, and a multisectoral rally at Roxas Avenue in Davao City. (AMU, DAA)
